title: The Phantom Plateau
AN EASILY COPIED INK FOR GRAPHIC RECORDERS
A Conjunctive Schedule of Reinforcement
abstract: Two pigeons were trained on a 15-minute, fixed-interval schedule. They were then trained on the conjunctive fixed-interval, fixed-ratio schedule, in which a response is reinforced only after the passage of a specified time and the emission of a minimal number of unreinforced responses. The period of time was kept at 15 minutes, while the number requirement was varied from 10 to 240 responses. Increasing the number requirement had the effect of decreasing the average rate of responding. The presence of the number requirement also changed the patternof responding within the 15-minute period from that obtained with ordinary fixed-interval reinforcement.

title: Operant Extinction After Fixed-Interval Schedules with Young Children
abstract: Four preschool children (~4 years old) were trained on fixed-interval schedules (FI 20 s, FI 30 s, FI 60 s) using plastic trinkets and, at times, dispenser-motor hum as reinforcers. After several conditioning sessions (3–4 per child, spaced ~22–29 days), extinction was introduced following a brief sequence of programmed reinforcers on the trained FI. Extinction performance, plotted cumulatively, showed marked individual variability, with higher extinction response rates generally observed following longer FI schedules (e.g., ~84 responses/min after FI 60 vs. ~10 after FI 20), and no clear relation to baseline (operant-level) rates. Observational notes suggested that self-generated behaviors (e.g., counting, self-talk, toy manipulation) appeared to modulate extinction, potentially functioning as discriminative or competing stimuli. The paper argues that, compared with nonhuman preparations, children introduce uncontrolled, response-produced stimuli that can either sustain or suppress responding during extinction, motivating future studies to bring such variables under experimental control.

title: SPARK SUPPRESSION
A Method for Obtaining Psychophysical Thresholds from the Pigeon
abstract: A psychophysical method for measuring the pigeon’s absolute visual threshold, combining Bekesy’s human audiometric tracking technique with operant conditioning procedures is described. Pigeons peck one key (A) when a lighted stimulus patch is visible and another (B) when it appears dark. Pecking key A reduces stimulus intensity; pecking key B increases it. Correct sequences under variable-ratio and variable-interval schedules maintain stimulus control and drive the stimulus intensity to oscillate across the bird’s threshold, yielding a continuous graphical record. Special contingencies—such as penalties for incorrect pecks, enforced pauses when switching keys, occasional omission of light after reinforcement, and differentiated reinforcement for below-threshold vs. above-threshold conditions—enhance control and minimize artifacts like wandering thresholds. The procedure can be generalized to measure other sensory thresholds by substituting appropriate stimulus continua. Its applicability to both absolute and differential thresholds are discussed.

title: TENSION-GAUGE
The Behavioral Effects of Some Temporally Defined Schedules of Reinforcement
abstract: Pigeons were trained under reinforcement schedules defined by alternating periods during which a single response could be reinforced ($t_D$) with periods in which no reinforcement was available ($t_A$). The ratio $T = t_D/(t_D + t_A)$ was varied systematically while the total cycle length remained constant at 30 seconds. Four subjects were studied as $T$ was reduced from 1.00 (equivalent to a fixed-interval 30-second schedule) to values as low as 0.013. Decreases in $T$ produced marked increases in overall response rates and responses per reinforcement, and cumulative records shifted from patterns resembling fixed-interval performance to those characteristic of fixed-ratio or variable-ratio schedules. At the smallest values of $T$, some birds showed irregularities and pauses comparable to \"ratio strain.\" Interresponse-time distributions revealed a progressive increase in the relative frequency of short IRTs with decreasing $T$. The results demonstrate that interval-like and ratio-like performances can be obtained within a single framework of temporally defined variables, and that systematic changes in limited-hold duration generate a transition from interval to ratio behavior.

title: NEW INK FOR CUMULATIVE RECORDERS
A DEVICE FOR MEASURING AND PROGRAMMINGTHE SPEED OF EXECUTION OF A SINGLE RESPONSE
abstract: his technical note describes an electrical circuit for measuring and controlling the speed or force of an operant response involving rotary motion. A small direct-current generator attached to a rotating lever or wheel produces an electrical output proportional to the subject’s response speed or mechanical energy. This signal biases a transistor–thyratron relay system that triggers when the generator output exceeds a preset criterion, thereby enabling the experimenter to program reinforcement or record responses based on movement velocity. Adjustable resistors permit calibration of response thresholds, while a smoothing capacitor stabilizes relay operation. The system offers a simple and inexpensive means to study quantitative response characteristics—such as vigor, force, or speed—in addition to response frequency, broadening the measurement of operant performance.

title: The effects of deprivation upon temporally spaced responding
abstract: Five rats and a rhesus monkey were trained to space their responses at least 20 seconds apart. The performances of the monkey and one rat were tested after five periods of deprivation ranging from zero to 72 hours and 9 to 69. 5 hours, re-spectively. Two rats received a 10-hour test session during which the accumu-lation of reinforcements produced satiation. Two other rats were trained to spacetheir responses by at least 20 seconds but not more than 24 seconds. The last twoanimals were also tested in a 10-hour satiation session.In all cases the major effect upon performance of manipulating deprivation inthe DRL situation was observed to occur only after short deprivations or when theanimals were near satiation. With greater satiation, long IRT' s became more fre-quent and response rates dropped. Over a wide range of deprivations, little changein the performance could be detected.

title: A SIMPLE WAY TO RECORD LATENCIES
Diagramming Schedules of Reinforcement
abstract: A graphical method for representing schedules of reinforcement is described. Cumulative records of responding are used as coordinates, with reinforcement specified by lines relating responses to time. The system depicts ratio and interval schedules, as well as their variable, alternative, conjunctive, interlocking, tandem, chained, mixed, and multiple forms. The method provides a compact notation for analyzing contingencies of reinforcement and suggests possible extensions to aversive control and punishment.

title: DIAGRAMMING SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
abstract: This brief methodological note introduces a graphical system for representing reinforcement schedules using cumulative-response coordinates, with number of responses on the y-axis and elapsed time on the x-axis. Skinner shows that each basic schedule—fixed ratio (FR), variable ratio (VR), fixed interval (FI), variable interval (VI), extinction, and continuous reinforcement—can be visualized as a line or region on this graph, where a response is reinforced when the cumulative-response curve contacts the line. The method extends naturally to more complex arrangements such as alternative, conjunctive, interlocking, tandem, chained, and multiple schedules, allowing their defining contingencies to be depicted as geometric relations between response number and time. Skinner suggests that such diagrams clarify relations among schedule types and may support future notational systems for escape, avoidance, or punishment schedules.

title: Avoidance Behavior and the Development of Gastroduodenal Ulcers
abstract: Eight rhesus monkeys were studied in a yoked-chair avoidance procedure in which one animal could postpone footshock for both members of the pair by lever pressing. Experimental animals developed stable avoidance responding, while yoked controls received identical shock exposure without control over its occurrence. Over weeks of continuous testing, all avoidance animals developed severe gastroduodenal ulceration, while controls did not. Measures of corticosteroid excretion showed no consistent elevations. The findings suggest that the behavioral contingencies of avoidance, rather than physical shock exposure alone, may be critical in the etiology of gastrointestinal pathology under conditions of prolonged stress.

title: Effects of Chlorpromazine and Promazine on Performance on a Mixed Schedule of Reinforcement
abstract: Drugs are known to alter operant behavior, yet their influence on discriminations without explicit external cues was less defined. This study examined the effects of chlorpromazine and promazine on pigeons responding under a mixed FI 15/FR 50 schedule. Four birds were maintained at 80% body weight and tested across repeated daily sessions, with drug or control injections administered prior to performance. Under control conditions, stable responding developed, including second-order effects where FI pauses varied depending on preceding schedule components. Both drugs reduced the characteristic postreinforcement pauses in fixed-interval components, with promazine at higher doses producing striking increases in overall response output compared to chlorpromazine. Importantly, drug effects selectively disrupted subtle schedule-controlled discriminations while leaving gross discriminations and ratio performance largely intact. These findings underscore the utility of complex schedules as analytic tools for detecting differential drug effects on behavioral organization.

title: The Grooming Behavior of the Chimpanzee as a Reinforcer
abstract: Grooming is a pervasive primate social behavior, yet its potential function as a reinforcer had not been directly tested. A young chimpanzee was provided access to grooming the experimenter’s arm contingent upon correct visual discrimination responses. Thirty-second periods of grooming, signaled by a clicker, reliably maintained responding, and the animal acquired both the original discrimination (square vs. cross) and a subsequent reversal. Despite its immature age, the subject showed strong motivation for grooming, likely amplified by extended social isolation. The study demonstrates that grooming, beyond its social and hygienic functions, can serve as an effective reinforcer for operant behavior. These findings extend the range of known reinforcers and suggest that species-typical social activities may be integrated into experimental analyses of behavior.

title: NEW TYPE OF CONNECTOR PLUGS AND SOCKETS
Stimulus-Producing Responses in Chimpanzees
abstract: Discrimination learning often requires not only food-producing responses (Rf) but also stimulus-producing responses (Rs) that bring discriminative cues under experimental control. Previous analyses inferred Rs indirectly, but this study directly examined them in chimpanzees. Using a two-key procedure, one key delivered food under fixed-interval or variable-ratio schedules (Rf), while the other produced red or blue lights correlated with reinforcement or extinction (Rs). Across multiple experiments, chimpanzees maintained substantial Rs rates, especially under fixed-ratio reinforcement of stimuli, and discriminations were strong (DRs near 1.0). Extinction or nondifferential stimuli rapidly abolished Rs performance, confirming that discriminative function—not mere stimulus onset—maintains responding. The work establishes Rs as operant behaviors governed by reinforcement schedules and provides an objective method for studying “observing responses.” These findings highlight Rs as essential behavioral processes for analyzing discrimination, attention, and conditioned reinforcement.

title: Some Factors Involved in the Stimulus Control of Operant Behavior
abstract: Stimulus control in operant behavior arises when reinforcement delivered in the presence of a discriminative stimulus (SD) alters the subsequent probability of responding. Earlier research had shown that temporal pairing of SD and reinforcement could produce generalization gradients, but the role of the operant response itself remained uncertain. This study tested whether stimulus–reinforcer pairing, independent of the response, was sufficient to establish stimulus control. Pigeons first received food on a variable-interval schedule in the presence of one color light but never in another. Later, key pecking was conditioned in white light, then extinguished while the colored lights alternated. Birds responded preferentially in the stimulus previously correlated with food, though less strongly than if responses had been differentially reinforced. These results confirm that temporal pairing of stimulus and reinforcement alone contributes to stimulus control, though direct response–stimulus contingencies sharpen the effect. The findings clarify boundary conditions for how discriminative stimuli acquire control of operant behavior.

title: PIGEON WATER SUPPLY
Probability Relations within Response Sequences Under Ratio Reinforcement
abstract: A procedure was developed for the purpose of investigating the internal cohesion of response sequences maintained on fixed-ratio reinforcement. Under this procedure, rats were trained in a two-lever Skinner box on a schedule wherein water reinforcement was delivered either upon the completion of N consecutive responses on lever A, or else upon the completion of a minimum of N consecutive responses on lever A followed by an additional response on lever B. A random programmer determined which of these two conditions prevailed on any run. The two main parameters investigated were N (the minimum number of responses required for reinforcement) and P (the probability that the animal is reinforced immediately upon the completion of the N responses on lever A). The values of N used were 4, 8, 12, and 16, and the values of P were 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75. The following two functions were calculated for the data of each animal for each of the four values of the variable to which it was exposed: (a) the probability of switching to lever B as a function of the number of responses already made on lever A, and (b) the frequency distributions of lengths of runs. The effect of increasing N was a shift in both of these functions upward along the abscissa, in such a way that the sharpest rise in function (a) and the median of distribution (b) always fell slightly above the stipulated value of N. The effect of increasing P was qualitatively similar to the effect of increasing N.

title: A SIMPLE PULSE SHAPER
Preference and switching under concurrent scheduling
abstract: A series of experiments is reported in which pigeons were trained to peck an illuminated key for grain. The color of this key was either red or green, and associated with each color was a given reinforcement schedule. Pecking on a second key permitted the birds to switch the color appearing on the first key. The general behavior resulting from this type of procedure suggested an operant chain in which pecking on the second key was maintained by its consequences for reinforcement on the first key. Preferences for a give color and rate of switching colors were found to be a function of the particular schedules and switching contingencies imposed.

title: Shock intensity in variable-interval escape schedules
abstract: When the intensity of the shock is raised or lowered for rats pressing a bar on a variable-interval escape procedure, the transition to a new rate is usually immediate. The rates are roughly proportional to the level of current but show more moderate positive acceleration from 40 to at least 400 microamperes.

title: SHOCK INTENSITY IN VARIABLE-INTERVALESCAPE SCHEDULES
process: Aversive control via negative reinforcement (escape) on variable-interval schedules; stimulus-intensity–response functions
abstract: Rats pressed a lever to terminate electric shock on VI escape schedules (typical mean: 30 s shock on, 120 s shock off). Using ascending and descending intensity series (0–400 µA) within single sessions, response rate shifted immediately with each intensity change. Rates were roughly proportional to current and showed positive acceleration from ~50 to 400 µA, with a “break” below 50 µA. Between-session drifts led the authors to estimate full intensity functions within single sessions. With precautions to prevent unintended avoidance, stable orderly performances were obtained; animals could be conditioned de novo at 50 µA and maintained on VI 30 s.

title: A source of error in estimating the number of reinforcements in a lever pressing apparatus

It is topically suspect — the note concerns the discrepancy between programmed/operated reinforcer-delivery (feeder/magazine) cycles and reinforcements actually obtained, not a lever-given-trough transition probability — and may not appear in the paper at all. Retained only as a low-confidence candidate pending scan-access confirmation.
abstract: Five male hooded rats were trained in a lever-pressing apparatus, food serving as reinforcement. Following two tourgh-training sessions, each subject was given three lever-pressing training sessions, a total of 150 reinforcements being given. A continuous record of lever and trough responses was obtained and subsequently analyzed. This showed that the probability of a lever response following a trough responses, i.e., p(L/T), as calculated over the final 40 reinforcements, ranges between 0.69 and 0.81. Furthermore, the probability is high that between the 50th and 110th lever response, subject engages in a response burst on the lever. This response bursts accounts for a considerable proportion of the difference between the total number of lever responses reinforced and the number of reinforcements obtained.

title: Some effects of temporal variables on conditioned suppression
authors: Stein, L., Sidman, M., & Brady, J. V.
abstract: The present experiment investigated two temporal variables in the Estes-Skinner conditioned suppression situation. The five animals were given prolonged training on a series of conditioned-suppression programs; the programs differed from each other with respect to the stimulus and between-stimulus durations. The degree of suppression varied widely from program to program. Roughly, programs in which the stimulus duration was short relative to the duration of the stimulus-off interval produced good suppression, and programs in which the stimulus duration was relatively long produced poor supression. These effects were largely reversible. "Relative Duration" defined as log(stimulus duration/stimulus-off duration), correlated 0.90 with the degree of behavioral suppression. The number of reinforcements obtained in each program was relatively constant at approximately 90% of the maximum number obtainable in an experimental session in spite of the wide differences in suppression. An estimate of the percentage of reinforcements that would be lost if the animal suppressed completely in the stimulus period was calculated for each conditioned-suppression program. This measure was correlated 0.92 with suppression scores, indicating that the strength of suppression in any program decreases to the extent that such suppression reduces opportunities for positive reinforcement.

title: Intermittent reinforcement of a complex response in a chimpanzee
abstract: The intermittently reinforced sequence was maintained with approximately the same number of "errors" as under continuous reinforcement. However, the percentage of sequences that did not conform to the reinforcement contingency decreased from 20% under continuous reinforcement to approximately 3% when 960 smissions of the reinforced sequence was required for an experimental session of 60 reinforcements, and 2% for the 1900 sequences required for an experimental sessions at a ratio of 33 to 1.

title: SCREW-ON MULTIPLE CONNECTORS
SOME NOTES ON "BURSTS"IN FREE-OPERANT AVOIDANCE EXPERIMENTS
process: Free-operant avoidance and conditioned suppression bursts
abstract: Sidman analyzed the occurrence of rapid, closely spaced response “bursts” in free-operant avoidance procedures where each lever press postponed shock for a fixed interval. Data from rats and monkeys showed that bursts often followed shocks or responses that terminated warning stimuli, though they also appeared after near-miss pauses that would have produced shocks. Early in training, bursts alternated with long pauses, resembling ratio-like performance patterns. Sidman proposed that bursts arise from the abrupt relief following aversive stimulation or warning termination, possibly through temporary broadening of stimulus generalization gradients. These observations suggested that shock onset, offset, and even its avoidance can all evoke short-lived increases in response probability.

title: OPERANT STUTTERING:THE CONTROLOF STUTTERING BEHAVIOR THROUGHRESPONSE- CONTINGENT CONSEQUENCES
process: Operant control of stuttering behavior — differential effects of punishment and escape (negative reinforcement) contingencies on speech disfluencies.
abstract: Three male stutterers (ages 15, 22, and 37) read aloud while every stutter produced either (a) a 1-second aversive tone (response-contingent punishment) or (b) 5 seconds of relief from a continuous tone (response-contingent escape). Stuttering increased when escape was contingent on stuttering and decreased—often to complete suppression—when tone onset followed stuttering. After aversive contingencies ended, compensatory bursts of stuttering occurred. Reading rate was largely unaffected, indicating that stuttering could be independently controlled as an operant distinct from speech rate. The findings supported an operant model of stuttering, in which reinforcement and punishment contingencies systematically modulate response frequency.

title: EDGE-MARKING OF RECORDING PAPER TO ELIMINATE CONFUSION OF RECORDS1
COUNTING BY HUMANS ON A FIXED-RATIOSCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
process: Human fixed-ratio performance and self-generated discriminative control
abstract: "Human subjects were asked to detect pointer deflections on a dial visible only when a key press produced a brief flash of light. Deflections were programmed on fixed-ratio (FR) schedules, and subjects’ light-flashing responses were recorded. One subject began counting the number of responses per ratio, producing an inverted-S pattern: high response rate post-reinforcement, a mid-ratio lull, and acceleration approaching reinforcement. When counting was explicitly instructed, similar positive acceleration near reinforcement was observed, confirming that verbal counting acted as a discriminative stimulus controlling response pacing. These findings show that human verbal behavior can serve as an internal “counter,” functionally analogous to external stimulus counters in animal FR performance."]

title: A NEW SHOCK GRID FOR RATS1
SOME EFFECTS OF NOISE ON HUMAN BEHAVIOR
process: Aversive control and discriminative control in humans — effects of response-contingent (escape/avoidance) versus noncontingent noise on operant behavior.
abstract: This study examined how intense noise affects human behavior under different contingencies. Participants performed fixed-interval and fixed-ratio observing tasks while noise was presented (a) noncontingently, (b) contingent on reinforcement, or (c) contingent on responses. Noncontingent noise produced only brief, transient disruptions, while response-contingent noise (as punishment or escape) reliably and stably modified performance—reducing, eliminating, or reorganizing response patterns. Discriminative use of noise (e.g., as a signal) also controlled responding independently of aversiveness. The results demonstrated that the behavioral impact of noise depends on its contingency relationship to responses or reinforcers, not on intensity alone, and that prior null findings likely stemmed from noncontingent stimulus presentations.

title: A Simple Stabilimeter
Erratum: The Effects of Deprivation upon Temporally Spaced Responding
THE EFFECT OF METHAMPHETAMINE ON OPERANT LEVELAND A VOIDANCE BEHA VIOR
process: Aversive control / avoidance conditioning with pharmacological modulation (psychopharmacology of operant behavior)
abstract: Across seven experiments with rats, methamphetamine reliably increased avoidance responding on Sidman-type schedules once the avoidance contingency had begun to control behavior; the drug did not comparably elevate unconditioned (operant-level) lever pressing. Dose–response data showed large transient rate increases at moderate doses (≈1–3 mg/kg), with temporary response suppression or cessation at higher doses (≥3–4 mg/kg) and evidence of short-term tolerance. Timing of administration (after avoidance came under control) was critical to observing rate increases. Control procedures (unavoidable shocks + time-out) indicated post–time-out rate surges after overdoses were drug-related rather than shock-induced. Findings dissociate stimulant effects on avoidance performance from general activity and highlight schedule parameters and response topography effec"This study examined how intense noise affects human behavior under different contingencies. title: THE EFFECT OF DEPRIVATION AND FREQUENCYOF REINFORCEMENT ON VARIABLE-INTERVAL RESPONDING
process: Motivational control (food deprivation) interacting with operant performance under interval schedules (schedule control)
abstract: Nine male rats pressed a lever for 0.045-g pellets on VI 1-min, VI 2-min, or VI 3-min schedules while daily deprivation was manipulated by testing at seven times since feeding (1–23 h). Stable performance was first established, then response rates were measured across deprivation times. Both deprivation and reinforcement frequency increased rate, with a significant interaction: equal increases in deprivation produced larger rate increases on richer VI schedules. Across deprivation levels, rates under different VIs were approximately proportional (e.g., r(VI-1) ≈ 1.35·r(VI-2); r(VI-1) ≈ 2.43·r(VI-3)), suggesting a multiplicative relation between deprivation effects and schedule value.

title: SEQUENTIAL DEPENDENCIES OF THE LENGTHS OFCONSECUTIVE RESPONSE RUNS
process: Response patterning and sequential dependency under ratio-like contingencies; extinction-induced variability
abstract: Three water-deprived rats responded on two levers where a minimum of eight consecutive responses on lever A followed by one on lever B produced water. Successive run lengths (number of A presses per run) were analyzed for sequential dependencies. The length of a given run covaried positively with the length of the preceding run, indicating first-order sequential effects. Visual inspection of run-by-run records also suggested cyclic fluctuations in run lengths across time. During extinction, variability in run length increased sharply, consistent with prior findings on behavioral variability during nonreinforcement. The results show short-term dependencies and increased response variability when reinforcement ceases.

title: SUSTAINED PERFORMANCE DURING VERY LONGEXPERIMENTAL SESSIONS
process: FR components; induction and satiation effects
abstract: Two pigeons were maintained in continuous experimental sessions lasting up to 28 days under a multiple schedule: DRL 1-min (white key), FI 10-min (green), and FR 50 (red). The DRL component sustained low, steady response rates, while FI and FR components alternated hourly to maintain overall responding and body weight. Over days and weeks, pigeons exhibited stable lever-pecking patterns similar to those in conventional daily sessions. Performance decrements occurred only with satiation or minor loss of stimulus control. Induction among schedule components occasionally produced cross-schedule rate changes. The study demonstrated the feasibility of continuous, around-the-clock operant performance, providing a baseline for long-term behavioral and physiological research.

title: BEHAVIOR UNDER EXTENDED EXPOSURE TO A HIGH-VALUEFIXED INTERVAL REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULE
process: Fixed-interval performance and temporal patterning under extended exposure
abstract: Three White Carneaux pigeons were exposed to a fixed-interval (FI) 30-minute schedule for over 2300 total hours (up to 146 sixteen-hour sessions). Extended observation revealed a rich progression of fixed-interval patterns beyond early “scalloping.” With continued training, birds displayed multiple forms of double and triple scallops, sustained “break-and-run” patterns, negative acceleration before reinforcement, and occasional scallops occurring independently of reinforcement delivery. These phenomena extended and refined earlier analyses by Ferster and Skinner, demonstrating that long-term FI exposure produces increasingly complex temporal structures in responding. One subject died near the end of the study, with its final session suggesting physiological deterioration. The findings highlight behavioral stability and emergent temporal organization under extreme duration FI conditions.

title: Behavior under extended exposure to a high-value fixed interval reinforcement schedule*
BY-PRODUCTS OFA VERSIVE CONTROL
process: Aversive control and conditioned suppression/facilitation; adventitious chaining between concurrent operants
abstract: Sidman examined how aversive control spills over onto “irrelevant” behavior in rhesus monkeys responding on concurrent schedules. A food-maintained operant (Lever A or chain pull; typically VI 4-min, later FR) ran alongside a Sidman avoidance operant (Lever B; R–S = 20 s). A warning stimulus periodically preceded unavoidable (“free”) shock. Initially, the pre-shock stimulus facilitated both responses, contradicting simple conditioned suppression. Sequence analyses showed frequent A→B alternations, implying adventitious chaining whereby the food operant acquired avoidance functions. Replacing A with a chain and, critically, switching A to fixed ratio broke A→B chaining, yielding the canonical pattern: suppression of the food operant during the pre-shock stimulus while the avoidance operant was facilitated. Results highlight superstitious linkage across response classes as a by-product of aversive control.

title: FIXED-RA TIO SCHEDULES OF CONDITIONEDREINFORCEMENT WITH CHIMPANZEES1
process: Conditioned reinforcement; fixed-ratio performance (post-reinforcement pause & running rate); discriminative chaining across conditioned reinforcers
abstract: Two 7-year-old chimpanzees earned poker chips (conditioned reinforcers) on fixed-ratio (FR) schedules by pressing a key under a white light; chips could be exchanged for food only when a red light appeared (session end). After FR 30 baselines, the ratio was raised (to FR 100; later FR 125), with sessions up to 8 h or 60 chips. Performance showed classic FR structure: post-reinforcement pauses and high, stable running rates that increased with ratio size. At high FR values, very long initial pauses dominated early session segments, yet once running began, rates were sustained (≈2–4 resp/s). Extinction produced bursts at prior running rates. Providing 50 chips at session start abolished the initial pause, supporting a chained-schedule/discriminative control interpretation of conditioned reinforcement."Sidman examined how aversive control spills over onto “irrelevant” behavior in rhesus monkeys responding on concurrent schedules. title: INTERACTION AMONG COMPONENTS OF AMULTIPLE SCHEDULE
abstract: Two male albino rats worked on a 4-component multiple schedule cycling every 5 min: FI 5-min (food; limited hold 2 min), SΔ1 (extinction), Sidman free-operant avoidance (tone), and SΔ2 (clicker). Across phases the avoidance interval (S-S and R-S) was 20 s, 5 s, avoidance extinction, then 10 s. Shortening the avoidance interval increased avoidance responding and elevated response rates during both SΔ components—demonstrating cross-component interaction. FI rates were idiosyncratic (one decreased, one unchanged). An immediate shift to 5 s produced a transient loss of stimulus control with near-equal rates across components; with continued exposure, typical FI scallops re-emerged and SΔ responding showed temporal patterning (late in SΔ1, early in SΔ2). During avoidance extinction, SΔ responding quickly declined despite initially high avoidance rates."Two 7-year-old chimpanzees earned poker chips (conditioned reinforcers) on fixed-ratio (FR) schedules by pressing a key under a white light; chips could be exchanged for food only when a red light appeared (session end). title: The use of pinch as an aversive stimulus
GENERALIZA TION GRADIENTFOR AUDITORY INTENSITY IN THE RAT
process: Stimulus generalization under operant discrimination (auditory intensity); gradient sharpening with discrimination; extinction generalization
abstract: Male albino rats lever-pressed under an auditory intensity discrimination using a 4-kHz tone. After establishing SD–SΔ differing by 40 dB, Phase II introduced four nonreinforced test intensities (SΔ and +/–10, +/–20, +/–30 dB toward SD) while SD continued on a VI-like geometric schedule (mean 59 s). Generalization gradients (responses per 7.5 min) across three 6-day blocks were concave/decelerated and well fit by hyperbolae; slopes sharpened with continued discrimination training (greater suppression at SΔ-proximal values). In extinction (no reinforcement for any intensity, 12 days), overall rates dropped and gradients flattened, yet graded responding persisted until near zero. Gradients were governed by distance from SD, not direction (attenuation vs increase). Results mirror classic generalization findings across operant/respondent paradigms.

title: INTERMITTENT REINFORCEMENT OF OPERANTBEHA VIOR IN CHILDREN'
authors: Long, E.R.; Hammack, J.T.; May, F.; Campbell, B.J.
abstract: ~200 children (ages 4–8) responded on keys/manipulanda in 20–30 min sessions (typically weekly) under FR, FI, and VI schedules with tangible reinforcers (trinkets, pennies) and sometimes projected pictures. Basic schedule effects resembled those in nonhuman labs (e.g., VI steady rates; FR ratio-run; FI scallop initially), but FI scalloping in children was often transient, giving way to steady or irregular rates. Performance was highly sensitive to reinforcer value and schedule programming: changing trinket type/amount, adding pictures at reinforcement, swapping VI interval sets (“tapes”), lengthening intersession intervals, or seeding brief FRs before FI could elevate rates and reduce pausing/grain. Social/contextual factors and weak deprivation constrained control. Overall, standard schedules can reliably organize children’s free-operant behavior, with notable reinforcer- and context-dependencies

title: RESPONSE TO DIFFERENT DEGREES OF NOVELTY:THE INCIDENCE OF VARIOUS ACTIVITIES'
abstract: Thirty male hooded rats were observed for 15 min in one of three test cages that differed in degree of novelty relative to home cages: N-1 (striped walls), N-2 (striped walls + wire-mesh floor), N-3 (N-2 + ~73 dB white noise). Using a 6-s time-sample, observers coded sniffing (S), locomotion (W), grooming (G), freezing (F), lying (L), and miscellaneous (M). As novelty increased, sniffing decreased and grooming increased; locomotion declined over time in all groups; freezing tended to rise later in sessions for a subset of rats. Patterns evolved across five 3-min blocks, with stronger progressive changes under higher novelty. Results challenge “exploratory” vs. “fear” drive accounts and suggest analyzing novelty effects via stimulus cues, arousal, and existing response strengths.

title: EFFECTS OF SCOPOLAMINE ON A MULTIPLESCHEDULE
abstract: Three food-deprived male albino rats performed on multiple schedules while receiving intraperitoneal scopolamine hydrobromide (0–1.6 mg/kg). Two rats worked on a 4-ply multiple: FI 5-min (limited hold 2 min) food, SΔ (no programmed consequence), Sidman avoidance (R-S = S-S = 20 s, 0.4-s, 2-mA shock), SΔ. A third rat worked on a 2-ply (FI vs SΔ). Scopolamine decreased FI response rate and reduced FI quarter-life toward ~1.25 min (flattened scallop), increased SΔ responding (discrimination disruption), and in avoidance raised shock frequency: low doses increased both avoidance rate and shocks (poorer temporal control), high doses depressed avoidance below baseline. One rat showed tolerance across repeated 0.1 mg/kg doses. Authors interpret effects as combined depressant action plus loss of stimulus control consistent with “amnestic-like” disruption in rats.

title: SOME OBSER VA TIONS ON AN OPERANT IN HUMAN SUBJECTS ANDITS MODIFICA TION BY DEXTRO A MPHETA MINE'
process: Schedule-controlled human operant behavior; drug effects on temporal control (DRL-like timing) and response rate/distribution
abstract: Seven male medical students pressed a telegraph key for nickels under a compound contingency combining fixed ratio and DRL: reinforcement occurred on the nth response only if each counted response followed the prior response by ≥ x s (non-qualifying responses reset the IRt timer). Two parameter sets were tested: FR100@DRL 2.5 s and FR10@DRL 25 s. Inter-response-time (IRT) distributions peaked just above the minimum delay; subjects were more efficient and steadier at 25 s than 2.5 s. After 5 mg dextro-amphetamine (vs placebo), IRT distributions shifted left (shorter IRTs) with little change in total reinforcers earned. Results replicate classic amphetamine effects seen in animals—tendency toward shorter IRTs—within a verbally instructed human operant preparation.

title: THE A CCENTUA TION OF A RATE DIFFERENCEDURING EXTINCTION
process: Resistance to extinction; differential persistence of responding under multiple schedules
abstract: Four male pigeons were trained under a multiple VI 3-min VI 9-min schedule with distinct keylight colors signaling each component. Two deprivation levels (≈75% and ≈90–95% body weight) were alternated across days. Under reinforcement, rates were typical for VI performance and slightly higher in VI 3 than VI 9, with deprivation increasing overall rates but not the ratio between components. During extinction, responding declined smoothly but persisted longer and at higher initial rates in the stimulus previously correlated with VI 3, producing a marked accentuation of the prior rate difference (e.g., VI3/VI9 ratios ≈1.2 under reinforcement vs. up to 3–4 during extinction). Experienced pigeons showed greater persistence. The findings illustrate stimulus–schedule interaction effects revealed in extinction.

title: FIXED-INTERVAL REINFORCEMENT OF RUNNINC IN A WHEEL
process: Fixed-interval schedule performance; temporal patterning of continuous operant behavior
abstract: Two rats were reinforced for running in a wheel on a fixed-interval 5-minute (FI 5) schedule, with a 6-watt light as the discriminative stimulus. Each session included pre- and post-interval periods of unreinforced running in darkness to compare spontaneous and schedule-controlled activity. Initially, running showed brief bursts and erratic pauses, but stable FI scallops later emerged—characterized by postreinforcement pauses followed by acceleration in running and sometimes deceleration near reinforcement. Increasing wheel friction (20–100 g) reduced overall rates, lengthened pauses, and eliminated late-interval deceleration, likely reflecting reduced magazine checking. Extinction revealed orderly decline in running and reappearance of unreinforced patterns. The study demonstrates that continuous responses like running can form fixed-interval patterns analogous to discrete operants such as lever pressing.

title: AN INTERMEDIA TE RESTRAINING DEVICE FORWORKING WITH MONKEYS'
abstract: Findley describes a restraining and harness system that provides a practical compromise between complete restraint and freedom for monkeys in operant research. The device consists of adjustable neck and waist collars attached to a pivoted harness, allowing limited movement (leaning, slight rotation, partial standing) while maintaining stable positioning in either a home stand or working chair. The working chair design also enables reliable electric shock delivery via conductive studs in the waist collar and an electrically isolated pivot rod, ensuring consistent contact through hair without tight fitting. The system allows for rapid transfer (~2 minutes) between stands, single-operator handling, secure drug injection, weighing, and maintenance of multiple monkeys efficiently."Two adult male rhesus monkeys responded on a multiple FI 2-min / FR 40 schedule for water (0.5 cc) with component-correlated lights. After stable baseline, secobarbital (e.g., 30 mg/kg, s.c.) produced three phases: (1) a brief stimulant period (FI pause loss; high, erratic rates), (2) an overall depressant phase (near-abolition of FI; FR broken into high-rate bursts separated by pauses), and (3) a post-depression excitatory phase where FR normalized sooner, while FI remained disrupted (little pausing, rough grain, late return of scallops). Larger doses lengthened/intensified these phases. Results replicate schedule-dependent barbiturate sensitivity: FI is more affected than FR. Verhave notes that FI disruption in the late phase could reflect impaired discrimination, tempering claims that barbiturates neatly “fractionate” tandem FI-FR components."Two water-deprived rats worked on a multiple schedule alternating FR 26 (clicking) and FI 4-min (tone). After stable baseline, rats received i.p. injections of atropine, benactyzine, or scopolamine (various doses). Cumulative records and average rates (per half-session) were compared to multi-session controls via drug/control ratios. High doses of all three anticholinergics disrupted temporal patterning: FI scallops disappeared (steady, moderate responding) and FR pauses/runs degraded; overall FR rates fell, whereas FI mean rate sometimes did not decrease because drugs reduced the usual post-reinforcement pause despite lower terminal rates. Medium doses often altered FI with little FR change (differential sensitivity). Low doses produced slight rate increases without pattern loss. Benactyzine effects were shorter-lived; scopolamine low doses could elevate FI rate. Authors note the multiple performance was partly governed by sequence rather than pure stimulus control.

title: OPERANT-LEVEL LEVER PRESSING BY A MONKEY AS A FUNCTIONOF INTER TEST INTERVAL
abstract: A naïve Cebus monkey was tested for spontaneous (“operant-level”) lever pressing across 252 half-hour sessions under varying intertest intervals of 15, 39, and 63 hours. Lever presses produced no programmed consequences. Responding decreased with repeated daily tests but recovered as the intertest interval increased, indicating a time-dependent recovery of baseline operant activity. Across four replications, lever-press frequency was consistently highest at the 63-hour interval. Analyses revealed significant effects of both intertest interval and replication, suggesting that nonreinforced lever pressing in monkeys may recover with rest rather than extinction reversal. The pattern was consistent with temporal spacing effects previously observed in rats.

title: SOME TIME-CORRELATED REINFORCEMENT SCHED ULESAND THEIR EFFECTS ON BEHAVIOR
process: Schedule control; transition from interval-like to ratio-like performance via temporally defined contingencies
static-equation-definitions: R = overall response rate; T = the time-correlation parameter, defined as the proportion of the cycle during which reinforcement is available, T = t^{D}/(t^{D}+t^{A}), where t^{D} is the reinforcement-available window and t^{A} is the no-reinforcement window (only the first response in t^{D} was reinforced); a, b = fitted constants of the power function (estimated for the 2-min cycle condition).
abstract:
Key-pecking by pigeons was reinforced under time-correlated (T) schedules in which a cycle alternated a reinforcement-available window (tᴰ) and a no-reinforcement window (tᴬ); only the first response in tᴰ was reinforced, otherwise the reinforcer was missed. With cycle lengths of 2 min and 10 min, T = tᴰ/(tᴰ+tᴬ) was decreased systematically. As T decreased, behavior shifted from interval-like (scalloped) to ratio-like: overall rate and short IRTs increased, initial–terminal rate differences shrank, and extinction resembled that after ratio schedules. Very small T values produced missed reinforcers and rate drop. Rate’s SD scaled linearly with mean rate. Prefeeding reduced output in a stepwise manner (ratio-like).
