title: THE MAINTENANCE OF BEHA VIOR BY THE TERMINA TIONAND ONSET OF INTENSE NOISE
process: Negative reinforcement; stimulus control by aversive-stimulus offset/onset; schedule interactions
abstract: Rats pressed and released a lever under two aversive-sound procedures: (1) Escape (Keller)—a press (Rᴾ) during 108–116 dB broadband noise terminated the noise and produced a silent period (T₀), after which noise returned; presses during T₀ had no effect. (2) Termination–Onset (Hefferline)—Rᴾ terminated noise and a lever release (Rᴿ) turned it back on. Abrupt noise offset maintained higher escape rates than slow offset. Varying T₀ from 2–20 s had little effect on overall escape rate (except very short values), though responses clustered early in T₀. Amphetamine (2 mg/kg) markedly increased both Rᴾ and Rᴿ rates. Long layoffs (days–years) transiently elevated escape rates. In the Hefferline schedule, Rᴿ showed a warm-up; Rᴾ did not—supporting partly independent control of the two operants.

title: SOME NEURAL AND BEHAVIORAL CORRELATES OF ELECTRICALSELF-STIMULATION OF THE LIMBIC SYSTEM
authors: Porter, R.W.; Conrad, D.G.; Brady, J.V.
process: stimulus control by site-specific neural events.
abstract: Nine rhesus monkeys received chronically implanted bipolar electrodes in limbic and related areas (septum, hypothalamus, anterior thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, median forebrain bundle, etc.). After lever-press training, animals earned brief brain shocks (self-stimulation) while concurrent EEGs were recorded. Self-stimulation of septal/anterior hypothalamic/anterior thalamic sites reliably produced spike-and-slow-wave complexes (often septal) correlated with high lever-press rates. Hippocampal stimulation often evoked focal seizure discharges: sessions showed bursts of pressing followed by EEG seizure “breaks”; as seizure duration waned within a session, pressing declined until seizures reappeared. Amygdala stimulation at higher intensities (≈15–20 mA) induced seizures that suppressed responding for long periods. Results link site-specific EEG patterns to maintenance—or suppression—of self-stimulation behavior.

title: SOME OBSERVATIONS ON AN OPERANT IN THE OCTOPUS
process: Operant conditioning ; shaping; extinction; schedule effects
abstract: Three Octopus vulgaris were shaped to pull a vertical lever that turned on a light; food (sardine pieces) was delivered at the opposite end of the tank contingent on lever operation. After stepwise shaping (approach → contact → lever operation), two animals showed reliable lever-pulling under continuous reinforcement across multiple sessions; fixed-ratio probes (FR 2–3) were briefly tolerated but increased latencies and produced breakdowns. When reinforcement was discontinued, responding declined with long pauses and session cessation—clear operant extinction; some spontaneous recovery occurred. A third animal exhibited competing behaviors (lamp grabbing, directed water jets) that interfered with stable responding. Results indicate the law of effect operates in O. vulgaris, suggesting wide phylogenetic generality of operant principles.

title: A COMPLEX CONCURRENT SCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENT
process: FI) schedule performance; schedule interaction/induction; response allocation
abstract: Two adult male chimpanzees worked on two keys concurrently: a right-key multiple schedule (FR→FI components) and a left-key VI schedule. With conc(VI 4, later VI 10; mult FR–FI) the animals often responded on both keys simultaneously (left hand on VI, right hand on mult). During transition to mult FR–FI, the FI component initially showed low, constant rates (little scalloping) while FR runs were typical. Extinguishing the left-key VI produced normal FI scallops on the right key; reinstating VI thereafter did not disrupt the established FI pattern. Very high FRs (up to FR 475) were sustained with brief pauses. Overall, the VI performance interfered with the development but not the maintenance of FI control; total reinforcement rate influenced right-key responding.

title: ONE BAR-PRESS PER DA Y:ACQUISITION AND EXTINCTION
abstract: Female hooded rats learned a single daily bar-press for food with the lever retracted immediately after each press. Two groups received 1 reinforced trial/day for 10 (E-10) or 50 (E-50) days, then 1 extinction trial/day for up to 75 days. A control group received only daily nonreinforced trials. E-50 reached a low, stable latency by extinction and showed no extinction across daily trials; E-10 largely matched this pattern (1 rat extinguished). In a second experiment, rats trained to criterion with 5 trials/day (≥5-min ITI) all extinguished within 60 extinction trials. Results show that immediate lever retraction alone does not prevent extinction; high trial spacing (≈1/day) is critical for maintaining responding without reinforcement.

title: SOME DATA ON BEHAVIOR REVERSIBILITYIN A STEADY STATE EXPERIMENT'
process: Steady-state response rate and behavioral reversibility
abstract: Three pigeons alternated repeatedly between two time-correlated reinforcement schedules differing in cycle length (tD + tA = 30.0 s vs. 0.94 s) while maintaining a constant proportion of deprivation (T = 0.05). Each schedule was continued until stable response rates were achieved, after which birds were switched to the alternate schedule—completing five full alternations. Response rates increased with shorter cycle lengths and remained roughly proportional across alternations. Although relative rates (ratios) stabilized after the first transition (≈0.65–0.84), absolute rates gradually increased across alternations, indicating partial but not complete reversibility of steady-state behavior. The findings suggest that steady-state response measures can be relatively recoverable across conditions, though subject to upward drift with repeated alternations.

title: INTER-RESPONSE TIME DISTRIBUTION AS A FUNCTION OFDIFFERENTIAL REINFORCEMENT OF TEMPORALLYSPA CED RESPONSES
authors: Kelleher, Roger, T.; Fry, W.; Cook, L.
process: Temporal discrimination and pacing under DRL / DRL-limited-hold schedules
abstract: Albino rats worked on DRL and DRL–limited-hold (DRL LH) schedules to study temporal discrimination via inter-response time (IRT) distributions and response-probability functions. Under DRL 20 LH 5, response probability stayed near zero for ~15 s after a press, then rose sharply around the reinforced window and declined beyond it; performances were precise and often produced long runs of consecutively reinforced responses. Removing response-produced auditory feedback slightly increased early IRTs but did not disrupt timing. Tightening the hold (DRL 20 LH 1) reduced percent reinforced yet maintained behavior. With DRL 20 (no LH, no feedback), timing was initially absent but developed across sessions. Similar precision emerged on DRL 18 LH 3, regardless of CRF or FR histories. Bursts and interim chains were largely absent."Three pigeons alternated repeatedly between two time-correlated reinforcement schedules differing in cycle length (tD + tA = 30.0 s vs. 0.94 s) while maintaining a constant proportion of deprivation (T = 0.05). Each schedule was continued until stable response rates were achieved, after which birds were switched to the alternate schedule—completing five full alternations. Response rates increased with shorter cycle lengths and remained roughly proportional across alternations. Although relative rates (ratios) stabilized after the first transition (≈0.65–0.84), absolute rates gradually increased across alternations, indicating partial but not complete reversibility of steady-state behavior. The findings suggest that steady-state response measures can be relatively recoverable across conditions, though subject to upward drift with repeated alternations.

title: THE ACTION OF A TROPINE, BENA CTYZINE, AND SCOPOLA MINEUPON FIXED-INTERVAL AND FIXED-RATIO BEHAVIOR
abstract: Two water-deprived rats worked on a multiple schedule alternating FR 26 (clicking) and FI 4-min (tone). After stable baseline, rats received i.p. injections of atropine, benactyzine, or scopolamine (various doses). Cumulative records and average rates (per half-session) were compared to multi-session controls via drug/control ratios. High doses of all three anticholinergics disrupted temporal patterning: FI scallops disappeared (steady, moderate responding) and FR pauses/runs degraded; overall FR rates fell, whereas FI mean rate sometimes did not decrease because drugs reduced the usual post-reinforcement pause despite lower terminal rates. Medium doses often altered FI with little FR change (differential sensitivity). Low doses produced slight rate increases without pattern loss. Benactyzine effects were shorter-lived; scopolamine low doses could elevate FI rate. Authors note the multiple performance was partly governed by sequence rather than pure stimulus control.

title: THE EFFECT OF SECOBARBITAL ON A MULTIPLESCHEDULE IN THE MONKE
process: Schedule-controlled performance under multiple FI/FR; drug effects on temporal patterning
abstract: Two adult male rhesus monkeys responded on a multiple FI 2-min / FR 40 schedule for water (0.5 cc) with component-correlated lights. After stable baseline, secobarbital (e.g., 30 mg/kg, s.c.) produced three phases: (1) a brief stimulant period (FI pause loss; high, erratic rates), (2) an overall depressant phase (near-abolition of FI; FR broken into high-rate bursts separated by pauses), and (3) a post-depression excitatory phase where FR normalized sooner, while FI remained disrupted (little pausing, rough grain, late return of scallops). Larger doses lengthened/intensified these phases. Results replicate schedule-dependent barbiturate sensitivity: FI is more affected than FR. Verhave notes that FI disruption in the late phase could reflect impaired discrimination, tempering claims that barbiturates neatly “fractionate” tandem FI-FR components."Two water-deprived rats worked on a multiple schedule alternating FR 26 (clicking) and FI 4-min (tone). After stable baseline, rats received i.p. injections of atropine, benactyzine, or scopolamine (various doses). Cumulative records and average rates (per half-session) were compared to multi-session controls via drug/control ratios. High doses of all three anticholinergics disrupted temporal patterning: FI scallops disappeared (steady, moderate responding) and FR pauses/runs degraded; overall FR rates fell, whereas FI mean rate sometimes did not decrease because drugs reduced the usual post-reinforcement pause despite lower terminal rates. Medium doses often altered FI with little FR change (differential sensitivity). Low doses produced slight rate increases without pattern loss. Benactyzine effects were shorter-lived; scopolamine low doses could elevate FI rate. Authors note the multiple performance was partly governed by sequence rather than pure stimulus control.

title: A NOTATION SYSTEM FOR THE DESCRIPTIONOF BEHAVIORAL PROCEDURES'
process: Formalization and symbolic representation of reinforcement contingencies and behavioral schedules
abstract: Mechner proposes a formal symbolic notation for describing behavioral procedures (schedules of reinforcement, contingencies, etc.) in a concise, logical, and diagrammatic format. The system integrates conventions from psychological paradigms, Boolean algebra, flow-chart notation, and mathematics to express stimulus–response–time relationships unambiguously. Examples include standard schedules (FI, DRL, Sidman avoidance, counting, conjunctive, interlocking) and complex procedures involving time intervals, response magnitude, and mathematical functions. Mechner demonstrates that the notation can facilitate classification of behavioral procedures and reveal formal parallels (e.g., DRL vs. counting schedules). The paper concludes that a standardized symbolic system could advance behavioral science by enhancing precision, communication, and theoretical analysis.

title: DELAYED MATCHING IN THE PIGEON
abstract: Pigeons performed delayed matching-to-sample (DMS) with a 1-s sample (flickering vs. steady white light), followed by a delay (0–10 s), then two keys (one flicker, one steady). A single grain delivery followed correct matches; correction trials repeated the same sequence but only first choices counted. In two birds, accuracy decreased monotonically with delay (~90–95% at 0 s to ~60–70% at 5 s). In two others, performance was higher but unstable—linked to stereotyped “mediating” behaviors during the delay that differed by sample type and appeared to guide choice. Birds lacking differentiated mediating chains showed orderly delay gradients. Results highlight the role of delay-period behavior in maintaining stimulus control over short delays.

title: A TECHNIQUE FOR DELIVERING SHOCK TO PIGEONS'
abstract: Azrin describes a method for delivering precise and reliable electric shock to pigeons via subcutaneous electrode implantation around the pubis bone. The electrodes connect to an external power source through a light harness and pulley system, allowing free movement without electrical variability. This approach eliminates problems associated with electrified grids (e.g., poor contact, escape responses, current inconsistency, feces shorting). Pigeons maintained normal performance under food-reinforced schedules, and response suppression occurred immediately when shock was delivered contingent on behavior. The technique provides consistent control of shock intensity and duration while preventing unintended escape responses, making it ideal for operant studies involving aversive control.

title: CONFIRMATION OF A POSITIVE RELATION BETWEEN DEPRIVATION ANDNUMBER OF RESPONSES EMITTED FOR LIGHT REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Segal tested whether food and water deprivation affected the number of responses rats emitted when lever presses produced brief light onset. Thirty-six male albino rats were divided into three deprivation levels (satiated, food-deprived, food + water-deprived). After 30 days of operant-level baseline sessions in darkness (no reinforcement), a single light-reinforcement session was introduced. While deprivation slightly decreased unreinforced (operant-level) bar pressing, it markedly increased responding when light onset was contingent on bar pressing, confirming Davis (1958)’s finding of a positive relation between deprivation and light-maintained responding. The results challenge interpretations based solely on general activity or drive and support the view that deprivation lowers thresholds to external stimulation.

title: INTERACTION BETWEEN THE COMPONENTS OF A CHAINED SCHEDULE
abstract: Hanson and Witoslawski examined how varying the fixed-ratio (FR) requirement in a chained fixed-interval fixed-ratio (FI FR) schedule affected responding during the FI component. Three food-deprived male Wistar rats pressed a lever for sweetened condensed milk under chain FI 4-min FR n schedules, where FR values were systematically changed (FR 5, 60, 120). As FR size increased, response rates during the FI component declined sharply and systematically, though their temporal distribution (scalloped pattern) was preserved. Total responses per reinforcement increased slightly with larger FRs, suggesting interaction beyond a simple inverse relation. The findings show that increasing response requirement in the terminal link reduces responding in the initial link, demonstrating strong interdependence between chained components.

title: Collection of temporal data with the duration tabulator1
AVOIDANCE RESPONDING AS A FUNCTION OF SIMULTANEOUSAND EQUAL CHANGES IN TWO TEMPORAL PARAMETERS
static-equation-definitions: Y = avoidance response rate (responses per unit time); X = the temporal parameter that was varied simultaneously and equally (the shock-shock and response-shock intervals of the Sidman free-operant avoidance procedure); 274.3 = empirically fitted constant; -1.1104 = empirically fitted exponent of the power-function regression. Equivalently log Y = log(274.3) - 1.1104 log X. NOTE: the surviving fragment 'Y=274.3X-1.1104' is genuinely ambiguous and is also readable as an ordinary linear regression Y = 274.3 X - 1.1104 (slope 274.3, intercept -1.1104); the power form is the more defensible reading (a negative exponent yields rate decreasing as the interval lengthens, consistent with avoidance) but cannot be confirmed against the scanned 1959 page image.
recursive-equation-definitions: Y = avoidance response rate (responses per unit time); X = the simultaneously and equally varied temporal parameter (shock-shock and response-shock intervals); 274.3 = fitted constant; -1.1104 = fitted exponent. This recursive field is a DUPLICATE of the static field: the catalog carried the single empirical equation across both fields rather than presenting two distinct models. Same linear-alternative caveat applies (Y = 274.3 X - 1.1104).
abstract: The nature of the relationship between rate of responding and the interval by whicheach response postpones an electric shock is reported. Throughout the experiment theshock-shock interval was varied simultaneously and kept equal to the response-shockinterval. Certain features of the inter-response-time distributions were also reported.

title: SOME BEHAVIORAL EFFECTS OF A TWO-VALUED,TEMPORALLY DEFINED REINFORCEMENT SCHED ULE
process: Variable-interval control under temporally defined (tD) two-valued schedules; schedule-controlled response rate and temporal patterning.
abstract: Eighteen pigeons (six groups of three) pecked under two-valued, temporally defined VI schedules in which cycles of 2.0 min and 0.5 min alternated randomly. Two parameters were manipulated: P (proportion of long cycles: 0.95, 0.90, 0.60, 0.40, 0.10, 0.05) and T (fraction of each cycle during which reinforcement could occur), with T stepped from 1.0 → 0.003125. Session rates (last 20 min of 30-min sessions) rose gradually across ~60–100 days and increased as T decreased, but the magnitude depended on P. Groups with P≈0.40 showed mixed-schedule-like temporal discriminations and large rate increases; P≈0.60 yielded low, linear rates resembling arithmetic VI with small T effects; extreme P’s behaved like fixed 2-min or 30-s schedules. Results clarify how simple two-interval mixtures can reproduce classic VI phenomena.

title: AN ANALYSIS OF THE BEHA VIOR OF RATS AND MONKEYSON CONCURRENT FIXED-RA TIO A VOIDANCE SCHED ULES
authors: Kelleher, Roger, T.; Fry, W.; Cook, L.
abstract: Rats (FR 50 or FR 200) and squirrel monkeys (FR 150) responded on concurrent schedules combining a fixed-ratio (FR) food program with Sidman (unsignaled) shock-avoidance (SS=RS=30 s; each response postponed shock 30 s). Control performance showed two alternating rates within each ratio: a low, stable “avoidance” rate immediately after reinforcement, then an abrupt shift to a high FR rate until food. To analyze component control and interaction, the authors ran avoidance extinction (no shock), FR extinction (no food), and prefeeding. Removing shock produced post-reinforcement pauses and predominantly high FR rates; removing food or prefeeding yielded predominant low avoidance rates. Monkeys’ avoidance was higher-rate and more extinction-resistant than rats’. Overall, components largely add without strong interaction.

title: A VERSIVE CONTROL WITH THE PIGEON'
abstract: The authors show that pigeons can acquire and maintain operant behavior under aversive control when reinforcement is shock termination/avoidance. After unreliable grid/foot methods, they introduce a robust wing-band electrode technique. Because shaping key pecks under shock was fragile (competing elicited reactions, immediate suppression when nonreinforced), they switch to a simpler, automatically shaped head-lifting response using a photocell beam: breaking the beam terminates pulsed shock (escape), and—with a 1-kHz tone CS 4 s before shock—can prevent shock (avoidance). Birds quickly acquire short-latency escape; avoidance emerges slowly across sessions but can reach high levels once criteria are incremented gradually. The paper provides a practical preparation for studying aversive reinforcement and avoidance in pigeons.

title: THE EFFECT OF RESERPINE ON THE CONDITIONEDEMOTIONAL RESPONSE IN THE GUINEA PIG
process: Conditioned emotional response (CER); suppression ratio as a function of aversive conditioning and pharmacological modulation (reserpine)
abstract: Twelve guinea pigs were trained to press a lever for water reinforcement on a variable-interval (VI) schedule and subsequently exposed to a conditioned emotional response (CER) procedure in which a clicker was followed by shock. The study examined behavioral suppression and the effects of reserpine at varying doses. Unlike rats, guinea pigs exhibited partial suppression of lever pressing during the conditioned stimulus and never drank during this period. Low doses of reserpine (0.003–0.004 mg/kg) markedly decreased overall responding and produced immobility during the clicker, while higher or chronic doses nearly eliminated lever pressing. The findings demonstrate both species-specific differences in CER behavior and the extreme sensitivity of guinea pigs to reserpine.

title: TITRATION BEHA VIOR ON VARIOUS FRACTIONAL ESCAPE PROGRAMS
abstract: Rats were trained to press a lever to produce fractional reductions in electric shock intensity under a “titration” schedule, in which shock intensity periodically increased in discrete steps. The study examined how response patterns varied with the rate of programmed shock increments and with ratio requirements for producing decrements. The median maintained shock level rose as the interval between increments shortened and as more responses were required per decrement, reflecting a higher response threshold and competing behavior under stronger aversive control. Wave-like oscillations in shock level and irregular responding emerged under certain parameters, suggesting analogies with psychophysical threshold behavior. The findings characterize titration schedules as a continuous, fractional form of escape responding.

title: Abstracts of the Conference on the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
DIFFERENTIAL DRUG EFFECTS UPON A THREE-PLYMULTIPLE SCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENT
process: Multiple-schedule operant performance (food-maintained CRF vs. Sidman avoidance vs. extinction) under pharmacological modulation.
abstract: Four food-deprived rats worked on a three-component multiple schedule—Extinction (SA), Continuous Reinforcement (CRF with sweetened milk), and Sidman shock avoidance (RS=SS=10 s)—repeated in 9-min cycles (13/day). Drugs were administered i.p. to test differential effects across components. Morphine (≈5–15 mg/kg) disrupted CRF at lower doses than avoidance; amphetamine (0.5–2 mg/kg) markedly increased rates in all components, especially SA, with “drinkometer” evidence of response–consumption dissociation; pentobarbital (8–24 mg/kg) produced biphasic effects with transient depressions followed by elevated SA; chlorpromazine (≥2–3 mg/kg) selectively impaired avoidance while sparing CRF at intermediate doses; MAO inhibitors (iproniazid, nialamide; high/extended doses) produced prolonged CRF disruption (“loss of appetite”) with comparatively minor effects on avoidance/SA. The preparation cleanly revealed drug-specific behavioral profiles.

title: A transistorized circuit for recording contact responses1
SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT AND DISCRIMINA TION LEARNING'
authors: Green, E.J.; Sanders, R.M.; Squire, R.W.
process: Human operant discrimination learning under different schedules of reinforcement
static-equation-definitions: DI = discrimination index; R_{S^D} = number of (lever-press) responses emitted in the presence of the discriminative stimulus S^D; R_{S^\Delta} = number of responses emitted in the presence of S^\Delta; R_{S^D} + R_{S^\Delta} = total responses across both stimulus conditions. DI is bounded 0-1, with 0.5 indicating no discrimination.
abstract: Seventy college students were tested in a visual discrimination task (1-2-5 light pattern) under 13 reinforcement schedules: continuous, fixed ratio (FR 5–20), variable ratio (VR 5–20), fixed interval (FI 5–30 s), and variable interval (VI 5–30 s). Each 1-hour session included 60 presentations (30 SD, 30 SΔ), with lever-press responses earning points under schedule control. Discrimination indices (SD responses / total responses) revealed that shorter ratios and intervals produced more rapid and stable discriminations. Longer ratios led to “ratio strain” and higher variability; longer intervals yielded flatter SD–SΔ separation and signs of temporal discrimination. The results indicated that human discrimination performance reflects response differentiation shaped by reinforcement contingencies, paralleling nonhuman data but bounded by fixed stimulus intervals.

title: Punishment and Recovery During Fixed-Ratio Performance
abstract: Six pigeons were trained on fixed-ratio (FR 10–50) schedules with food reinforcement, then exposed to immediate electric-shock punishment after each response. Shock intensity was systematically increased from 1 V to 120 V across 120 days. Punishment selectively lengthened postreinforcement pauses but did not reduce the local (terminal) response rate once responding began. Higher voltages prolonged pauses and reduced total responding, with recovery of performance occurring both within and across sessions. Even severe punishment (80–120 V) produced partial recovery, though early-session pauses remained extended. The results indicate that punishment in FR schedules primarily affects response initiation rather than rate, contrasting with generalized suppression seen in variable-interval schedules.

title: GENERA LIZA TION AND PREFERENCE ON ASTIMULUS-INTENSITY CONTINUUM
abstract: Pigeons pecked a small red key light while stimulus intensity varied over 11 steps (~3.6 log units). Experiment I (n=6): each bird was trained at a single intensity (continuous light), then tested without reinforcement as intensity swept up/down in 30-s steps. Generalization gradients were smooth, peaked near training intensity, sometimes asymmetric or slightly displaced; no evidence of a monotonic “brighter→faster” effect. Experiment II (n=4): birds were reinforced equally at all intensities (FI 1-min during test). A preference emerged for lower-middle intensities. The preference may partly explain asymmetries in single-intensity gradients; alternatively, summing identical gradients centered on each reinforced intensity approximated the observed preference.

title: A FLEXIBLE MODEL FOR GENERALIZATION GRADIENTS
abstract: Schlosberg describes a mechanical analog model of stimulus generalization that substitutes a physical apparatus for the behaving organism. The model uses movable ordinates (weighted bicycle spokes) on a graph representing stimulus values, with tensioned threads or wires forming a “generalization gradient.” Reinforcement and extinction are simulated by adding weights to specific ordinates. Adjusting the tension or stiffness of the connecting line reproduces empirical patterns reported in the literature—such as linear gradients (Solomon & Schlosberg, 1943), depressed gradients after repeated unreinforced tests (Pierrel, 1958), and curved, shifted peaks (Hanson, 1957). The model provides a flexible teaching and conceptual tool for exploring how reinforcement distribution and stimulus spacing determine generalization gradients.

title: THE PSYCHIATRIC NURSE AS A BEHAVIORAL ENGINEER'
abstract: Across multiple psychiatric wards, nurses implemented operant programs to reduce disruptive behaviors (e.g., office-intrusion, psychotic talk, violence, hoarding) and to strengthen deficits (e.g., self-feeding). Using time-sample observations and simple contingencies—primarily extinction of attention, differential reinforcement of incompatible/alternative behavior (DRI/DRA), fixed-interval “limited-hold” social reinforcement, escape/avoidance via mild food-spilling, and stimulus satiation (abundant magazines)—patients’ target behaviors changed over 6–11 weeks with 24/7 coverage. Case data show selective decreases in problem behavior (often via withdrawing nurse attention) and increases in adaptive responses (self-feeding maintained >10 months). Practical constraints (staff turnover, “bootleg” reinforcement) and staff attitudes are discussed, framing nurses as day-to-day behavior engineers."Schlosberg describes a mechanical analog model of stimulus generalization that substitutes a physical apparatus for the behaving organism. The model uses movable ordinates (weighted bicycle spokes) on a graph representing stimulus values, with tensioned threads or wires forming a “generalization gradient.” Reinforcement and extinction are simulated by adding weights to specific ordinates. Adjusting the tension or stiffness of the connecting line reproduces empirical patterns reported in the literature—such as linear gradients (Solomon & Schlosberg, 1943), depressed gradients after repeated unreinforced tests (Pierrel, 1958), and curved, shifted peaks (Hanson, 1957). The model provides a flexible teaching and conceptual tool for exploring how reinforcement distribution and stimulus spacing determine generalization gradients.

title: THE EFFECT OF CHANGING THE SCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENTUPON DURATION OF RESPONDING'
abstract: Schaefer and Steinhorst (1959) examined how changes in reinforcement schedules affect the duration of lever pressing (D) in rats. Eleven male rats were trained under continuous reinforcement (CRF) and later exposed to FR 5, FR 10, or shock-paired schedules. Lever press duration (D) was reliably measured using a microswitch system. Results showed that D was a stable, individual-specific characteristic under steady reinforcement but became unstable when the schedule changed (especially from CRF to FR 5). D increased immediately following schedule changes, often before rate changes appeared. Shock reduced both D and response output, while minor external disturbances had little effect. Findings highlight D as a sensitive microbehavioral index of reinforcement contingencies.

title: EFFECTS OF METHYLPHENIDYLACETATE AND CHLORPROMAZINEON CERTAIN COMPONENTS OF GENERAL ACTIVITY
process: Drug-induced modulation of operant and nonoperant behavioral components
abstract: Bindra and Baran (1959) analyzed how methylphenidylacetate (Ritalin) and chlorpromazine (Largactil) differentially affect specific components of rat general activity. Thirty-two male rats were observed after injections of three dosages of each drug, or saline control. Using timed observations, the researchers quantified sniffing, lying, grooming, and frequency of activity changes. Methylphenidylacetate increased sniffing and behavioral variability while decreasing lying; chlorpromazine produced the opposite pattern—reducing sniffing and activity changes but leaving lying and grooming largely unaffected. Effects peaked within 30–60 minutes and were dosage-dependent. The study demonstrated that analyzing discrete behavioral components yields greater sensitivity to pharmacological effects than gross activity measures.

title: THE RELATION OF AMOUNT OF REINFORCEMENT TO PERFORMANCEUNDER A FIXED-INTERVAL SCHEDULE
authors: Stebbins, W.C.; Mead, P.B.; Martin, J.M.
process: Effects of reinforcer magnitude on operant performance under fixed-interval schedules
abstract: Two food-deprived rats worked on an FI 2-min schedule while the amount of primary reinforcement was varied via sucrose concentration (5%, 12.7%, 32%, 50%; 0.02-ml dipper). After stable FI performance, each concentration was tested for 4 hours. Response rate increased with log sucrose concentration across the tested range: little change from 5%→12.7%, higher at 32%, and highest at 50% (contrary to prior VI findings of a downturn at high concentrations, likely due here to small reinforcer volume limiting satiation). Cumulative records and interval histograms showed concentration-related changes in within-interval distribution (“scallop”) with some evidence of sharper terminal responding at certain concentrations. Authors suggest an exponential rate-concentration relation under these parameters.

title: GENERA LIZA TION OF CONDITIONED SUPPRESSION'
abstract: Ray and Stein (1959) examined generalization of conditioned suppression along a tone-frequency continuum in rats. Lever pressing for milk on a VI 2-min schedule was suppressed by a 1800 Hz tone paired with shock (CS), while a 200 Hz tone (SA) signaled safety. Once discrimination stabilized, intermediate tones (560, 980, 1120, 1500 Hz) were presented during test sessions. Suppression ratios decreased systematically with increasing similarity to the CS, forming smooth gradients for two of three subjects. Results confirm that conditioned aversive control follows the same generalization principles as appetitive conditioning, demonstrating stimulus control of fear responses across auditory frequencies.

title: SUPPRESSION OF A PERFORMANCE UNDER DIFFERENTIALREINFORCEMENT OF LOW RATES BY APRE-TIME-OUT STIMULUS
abstract: Two rhesus monkeys worked on VI schedules that were progressively made less favorable (VI 6→VI 20; added DRL 5–30 s). A pre-time-out (red-light) stimulus occurred every 18 min with a limited-hold: any response in the final 5 s produced a 60-min time out (all lights/feedback off). Despite leaner reinforcement (and added DRL), the pre-time-out stimulus reliably suppressed responding near its end and animals avoided triggering time outs. Thus, time out functioned aversively across conditions; no evidence that time out became positively reinforcing as the baseline schedule was degraded.

title: A PRECISION LIQUID FEEDING SYSTEM CONTROLLEDBY LICKING BEHA VIOR'
abstract: Hulse (1959) describes a precision liquid-feeding apparatus for controlling fluid delivery contingent on a rat’s licking behavior. The system integrates a specially designed plexiglass drinking tube with a brass electrical contact, an electronic relay that detects each lick, and an infusion pump driven by a rotary solenoid to deliver precise drop volumes. A solenoid-driven lever retracts the fluid between licks to prevent unreinforced contact. The design allows fine control of liquid amount per lick, total consumption, and reinforcement schedules, enabling the use of licking as an operant response. The apparatus provides reliable, quantitative control over consummatory behavior for research applications in operant and taste conditioning.

title: A SIMPLE INTER VAL-PROGRAMMING CIRCUIT'
abstract: Clark and Caudill (1959) describe a low-cost interval-programming circuit for use with Gerbrands punched-tape or cam-timer systems. The design automates fixed-interval (FI), variable-interval (VI), and limited-hold schedules by coordinating relay-controlled lock-up and timing mechanisms. The circuit employs relays, resistors, capacitors, and diodes to control reinforcement availability and prevent premature responses, with adjustable parameters for timing reliability and discharge characteristics. The apparatus can also operate as a self-recycling or multiple-schedule timer. The authors provide detailed specifications for construction and calibration, emphasizing reliability, flexibility, and low expense (approx. $15–25 in 1959).

title: STIMULUS GENERALIZATION AS A FUNCTION OF THE TIMEBETWEEN TRAINING AND TESTING PROCEDURES
authors: Thomas, D.R.; Ost, J.; Thomas, D.
abstract: Thomas, Ost, and Thomas (1959) examined how time intervals between training and testing affect stimulus generalization in pigeons. After discrimination training with 550 nm (SD) and 570 nm (SΔ) lights, groups were tested 1, 7, or 21 days later. All groups showed peak responding at 540 nm, shifted away from SΔ, with gradients equally steep across time delays. Relearning sessions after 7 and 21 days revealed strong retention and minimal responding to SΔ. The results indicate that discrimination learning and the associated generalization gradient remain stable for at least 21 days without practice, contradicting prior findings that delay weakens gradients.

title: Arc Suppression in Shock Circuits1
SOME ELECTRONIC CONTROL UNITS FOR OPERANT BEHAVIOR STUDIES:I. A RESPONSE AND REINFORCEMENT CONTINGENCY TRANSLATOR'
authors: Schoenfiled, W.N.; Cumming, W.W.; Hearst, E.; Waine, M.; Snapper, A.G.; Haas, P.
abstract: Schoenfeld, Cumming, Hearst, Waine, Snapper, and Haas (1959) describe an advanced electronic “translator” unit for controlling and recording operant behavior contingencies. The system electronically processes response pulses, controls reinforcement timing, and interfaces with programming systems for flexible experimental design. It accepts response input, outputs to counters or recorders, and manages reinforcement availability via pulse gates, flip-flops, and one-shot circuits. The unit handles extremely high response rates (up to 100 kHz) and allows precise timing and manual testing through control switches and indicators. Accompanying Schmitt trigger circuits ensure stable operation. The design offers reliability, modularity, and versatility for complex temporal reinforcement schedules.

title: DISCRIMINA TION OF CHA NGES IN HEA R T RA TE:TWO UNSUCCESSFUL A TTEMPTS
abstract: Mandler and Kahn (1959) conducted two experiments to determine whether verbal behavior could be conditioned to changes in heart rate. In the first study, a subject attempted to label cardiac acceleration or deceleration (“FAST” or “SLOW”) with reinforcement. Apparent success was later shown to be based on respiratory changes correlated with heart rate (sinus arrhythmia), not direct cardiac discrimination. A second subject, instructed only to “guess” which of two lights would appear while reinforcement coincided with cardiac changes, performed at chance across 4,675 trials. The findings indicate that adults cannot easily discriminate or verbally respond to discrete cardiac rate changes, suggesting that “emotional” verbal behavior may rely on broader visceral cues.

title: HUMAN OBSERVING BEHAVIOR AFTER SIGNAL DETECTION
process: discriminated operant control and postreinforcement stimulus control
abstract: Laties and Weiss (1959) examined postreset observing responses (PRORs) in human subjects performing a signal detection task under fixed-interval schedules. Participants monitored a meter pointer that occasionally deflected and pressed one key to reset it and another to illuminate the dial. PRORs—key presses made shortly after a reset—were analyzed under four manipulations: (1) reinforcing PRORs increased their frequency; (2) adding an auditory signal to the reset reduced PRORs; (3) suggesting the reset key was unreliable increased PRORs; and (4) requiring use of one hand for both keys had no effect. Results indicate PRORs function as discriminated operants under control of post-reinforcement stimuli, demonstrating how reinforcement distinctiveness and uncertainty shape human observing behavior.

title: THE AVERSIVE CONTROL OF AN OPERANT DISCRIMINATION'
abstract: Appel (1960) examined whether rats’ Sidman avoidance responding (RS 20 s, SS 2 s) could come under stimulus control. A tone signaled SD (avoidance active); in SΔ the avoidance contingency was removed while unavoidable shocks were delivered at 0, 0.20, or 0.50 shocks/min. With no shocks in SΔ, rats acquired the discrimination via extinction of SΔ responding while SD rates stayed higher. Introducing unavoidable SΔ shocks prevented or degraded discrimination: SΔ responding rose (and often SD rose modestly), keeping SD vs. SΔ rates similar; in some animals prior good discrimination was impaired when shocks (even 1 every 5 min) were added to SΔ. Thus, unavoidable shocks in SΔ sustain responding and block discrimination based on aversive control.

title: OPERANT BEHAVIOR IN MENTAL DEFECTIVES:EXPLORATORY STUDIES'
authors: Ellis, N.R.; Barnett, C.D.; Pryer, M. W.:
abstract: Ellis, Barnett, and Pryer explored free-operant performance in institutionalized adults labeled “mentally defective” (historical term). Using a Lindsley manipulandum and candy (later cigarettes) as reinforcers with a 5-s time-out, Study 1 (N=12; IQ≤30) established lever pressing (CRF → FR 10) and compared FR 30, VI 1-min, FI 1-min, and extinction. Interval schedules produced erratic, pause-laden records; FR produced smooth, high, linear rates with pauses mainly post-reinforcement. Study 2 (N=26; IQ 30–70; MA 3–9 yr) escalated FR from 10 up to 1024: higher MA/CA predicted higher overall rates; many participants sustained very high ratios; reliability across days was good (odd–even ρ≈.95). Some “superstitious” adjunctive acts were noted. Authors suggest operant methods are feasible for training severely impaired populations.

title: BEHA VIOR STABILITY UNDER EXTENDED EXPOSURE TOA TIME-CORRELA TED REINFORCEMENT CONTINGENCY
abstract: Cumming & Schoenfeld examined how “steady state” behavior actually stabilizes under prolonged exposure to a time-correlated reinforcement schedule. Six pigeons (“birds”) worked for many months on a 30-s cycle with a limited-hold proportion T = 0.05. The authors tracked response rate day-by-day, evaluated common stability criteria (e.g., a 6-day ≤5% split-half rule), and compared early blocks to very long-run performance. They found sizeable within- and between-block variability, coefficients of variation ~19% across birds, and showed the 6-day rule often selects non-representative means. Typically 40–60 days were needed before block means bracketed the overall mean. After training, six 20-min extinction sessions produced bursts (“runs”) separated by pauses; extinction was relatively rapid. The paper argues for explicit, data-based stability standards in steady-state research.

title: INTERMITTENT REINFORCEMENT OF DISCRIMINA TIVEL Y CONTROLLEDRESPONSES AND RUNS OF RESPONSES'
process: Discriminated operant behavior under intermittent reinforcement
abstract: This study examined the effects of intermittent reinforcement applied to discriminatively controlled responses in rats. Following stimulus onset (light + tone), only a subset of bar presses—or runs of bar presses—were reinforced. Despite reduced reinforcement frequency, animals maintained clear stimulus control, though response latency increased and became more variable. The study established that discrete discriminative stimuli can sustain operant behavior under sparse reinforcement, bridging partial reinforcement paradigms in runway studies with operant methods.

title: SOME EFFECTS OF BRAIN STIMULATIONON TIMING BEHA VIOR
abstract: This study examined how electrical brain stimulation as a reinforcer affects differential reinforcement of low rates (DRL) timing behavior in rhesus monkeys. Monkeys with chronically implanted electrodes received either food or intracranial stimulation in regions such as the globus pallidus, medial forebrain bundle, and anterior thalamus. Brain stimulation in the globus pallidus disrupted temporal discrimination—shortening interresponse times and increasing response rates—while stimulation in other areas did not. The pattern closely resembled that produced by amphetamine administration, suggesting region-specific neural mediation of timing processes.

title: SOME ELECTRONIC CONTROL UNITS FOR OPERANT BEHAVIORSTUDIES: II. A RANDOM RATIO GENERATOR'
authors: Schoenfiled, W.N.; Cumming, W.W.; Hearst, E.; Snapper, A.G.; Haas, P.
process: Random ratio (RR) reinforcement — probabilistic control of operant responding
abstract: This technical note describes an electronic circuit for generating random ratio reinforcement schedules. The device uses a high-frequency pulse divided and shaped through amplifiers and a phantastron delay circuit to produce brief discriminable reinforcement opportunities (tᴰ) separated by variable intercycle intervals (tᴵ). The system yields an equal and independent probability of reinforcement for each response, simulating random ratio contingencies in operant experiments. The authors also discuss calibration and substitution of commercial delay generators for precision control.

title: A CONTINUOUS STENCIL DUPLICATOR'
abstract: Ferster describes the design and operation of a low-cost, continuous stencil duplicator capable of producing long strips of printed material, such as teaching-machine tapes, beyond the size limits of commercial presses. The apparatus modifies a standard spirit duplicator with a roller-and-belt superstructure, enabling continuous stencil rotation and long-roll paper feed. With proper alignment, it can yield over 100 copies of six-foot tapes at minimal cost. The paper and stencil materials are commercially available, making the system practical for experimental or instructional applications.

title: SPEECH RA TE METER FOR VOCAL BEHA VIOR ANAL YSIS
process: Human verbal behavior measurement and analysis
abstract: Starkweather introduces an automated device for quantifying vocal behavior by recording the rate of speech from audio input. The “Speech Rate Meter” detects speech pulses corresponding to syllabic or emphasized vocal elements, converts them to uniform electrical pulses, and produces cumulative records representing word rate over time. Validation showed a strong correlation (r = 0.988) between instrument readings and manual word counts across interview samples. The system can also simultaneously record a conversational partner’s vocal activity to study listener reinforcement effects. The apparatus provides an objective, operant-compatible measure of human verbal behavior.

title: THE BEHA VIORAL EFFECTS OF REPEATED EXPOSURE TOTHREE MIXED EXTINCTION SCHEDULES
abstract: Weissman examined how rats respond under repeated extinction conditions embedded within mixed fixed-ratio (FR 24), fixed-interval (FI 2-min), and differential-reinforcement-of-low-rate (DRL 20-s) schedules. Across months of training, stable “trained extinction” patterns emerged that differed sharply from one-trial extinction. Under mixed FR schedules, extinction began with a brief “priming run” followed by little or no responding; under FI, extinction showed abrupt cutoffs after initial runs; and under DRL, extinction contained long pauses interspersed with occasional high-rate bursts absent during reinforcement. Despite comparable stability, rats under DRL emitted far more extinction responses than under FR or FI, indicating weaker discrimination of extinction onset.

title: EFFECTS OF PUNISHMENT INTENSITY DURINGVARIABLE-INTER VAL REINFORCEMENT
process: Punishment (response-contingent aversive stimulation) interacting with schedule-controlled behavior
abstract: Six pigeons responded on VI 1-min food schedules while every key-peck also produced electric shock via implanted electrodes. Adding punishment (and stepwise increases from 10→40–60 V) produced immediate, strong suppression followed by gradual recovery within and across sessions; higher intensities reduced or eliminated recovery. Decreasing intensity yielded slow, days-long increases in responding; removing punishment caused brief “overshoot” above baseline. Response rate under punishment remained orderly (uniform VI-like), scaled inversely with intensity and directly with deprivation, and re-suppressed after brief no-punishment timeouts.

title: Suppression of a performance under differential reinforcement of low rates by a pre-time-out stimulus
ESCAPE AND A VOIDANCE RESPONSE OF PRE-SCHOOL CHILDREN TOTWO SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT WITHDRA WAL
process: Avoidance and escape behavior maintained by removal of positive reinforcement
abstract: Preschoolers viewed cartoons that periodically stopped (reinforcement withdrawal) unless they pressed a bar. Two contingencies were tested: (1) a Hefferline escape–avoidance schedule, where each bar press postponed the next interruption by n seconds, and (2) an “escalator” schedule, where each press added n seconds to the total delay before the next withdrawal. Both schedules established consistent responding: children rapidly learned to press to restore or maintain cartoons. Under the escalator schedule, bursts of responses alternated with plateaus, evolving into smooth avoidance patterns that minimized reinforcement loss. The study demonstrated that human avoidance responding could be maintained by the temporary loss of positive reinforcement.

title: OPERANT RESPONDING IN A HORSE UNDERSEVERAL SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
process: Operant conditioning under fixed-ratio and fixed-interval schedules of reinforcement
abstract: A 10-year-old horse was conditioned to nudge a lever with its snout to receive small grain reinforcers. After shaping under continuous reinforcement, the animal was exposed to fixed-ratio (FR 3–11) and fixed-interval (FI 1–3 min) schedules. The horse quickly acquired stable response patterns characteristic of other species—steady rates under ratio schedules and scalloped patterns under longer interval schedules. Despite no deprivation regimen, operant responding was maintained effectively, demonstrating that equine behavior could be systematically controlled and analyzed within a standard reinforcement framework.

TEMPORAL AND INTENSIVE PROPERTIES OF HUMAN VOCALRESPONDING UNDER A SCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Lane developed a method to measure human vocal operants (“oo” sounds) under differential reinforcement of low rates (DRL) schedules, recording both temporal and intensity properties. Subjects produced “oo” responses into a microphone that illuminated a viewing light when responses met DRL timing contingencies. Across sessions, response rates adjusted toward the rate that maximized reinforcement. Subjects showed either acceleration or deceleration in response rate depending on prior reinforcement history. Interresponse times shifted systematically, paralleling animal data, while response duration and intensity remained stable. This study demonstrated that human vocal behavior follows the same temporal dynamics as nonhuman operants under DRL control.

title: A MATHEMATICAL INDEX OF PERFORMANCE ONFIXED-INTERVAL SCHED ULES OF REINFORCEMENT
authors: Fry, W.; Kelleher, R.T.; Cook, L.
process: Fixed-Interval (FI) schedule performance and quantitative characterization of response acceleration
static-equation-definitions: I is the index of curvature; the fixed interval is divided into 4 equal parts (quarters). R_4 is the total (cumulative) number of responses emitted during the interval; R_1, R_2, R_3 are the cumulative numbers of responses emitted by the end of the first, second, and third quarters, respectively. The index equals the normalized area between the cumulative-response curve and the constant-rate diagonal. A constant response rate yields I = 0; positive values indicate positively accelerated (FI-scalloped) responding concentrated near the end of the interval, negative values indicate front-loaded responding. For n = 4 the index is bounded by -3/8 and +3/8 (i.e. ±(n-1)/2n), reaching +3/8 = 0.375 when all responding occurs at the very end of the interval.
recursive-equation-definitions: I is the index of curvature; n is the number of equal parts into which the fixed interval is divided; R_n is the total (cumulative) number of responses emitted during the interval; R_i (i = 1, 2, ..., n-1) is the cumulative number of responses emitted by the end of the i-th part. The index equals the normalized area between the cumulative-response curve and the constant-rate diagonal. It is 0 for a constant response rate, increases toward +(n-1)/2n (approaching +0.5 as n increases) as responding becomes concentrated near the end of the interval, and decreases toward -(n-1)/2n for front-loaded responding.

title: DECREMENT IN PERFORMANCE DURING PROLONGEDA VOIDANCE SESSIONS
process: Avoidance responding and performance degradation (fatigue) under prolonged exposure
abstract: Two rhesus monkeys were kept on a Sidman (unsignaled) avoidance schedule for seven consecutive days, pressing a lever to postpone electric shocks. Periodic fixed-interval (FI) 5-minute components were inserted to assess changes in temporal discrimination and operant control. Over the course of the week, avoidance response rates gradually declined and shock frequency increased, particularly after four days. Despite clear performance decrements, discrimination between avoidance and FI stimuli remained intact, and the typical FI scallop pattern persisted, though “flat” intervals (single or no responses) appeared more often. Observations suggested the monkeys could maintain minimal responding while dozing, indicating remarkable behavioral persistence despite fatigue and partial sleep deprivation.

title: SOME RELA TIONS BETWEEN THE A UDITOR Y SYSTEM OF THEMEDULLA AND AUDITORY-STIMULUS FUNCTIONS
authors: Harrison, J.M.; Abelson, R.M.; Fisher, G.L.
process: Auditory stimulus control and its disruption by neural lesions
abstract: This study examined how lesions to specific medullary auditory pathways (ventral acoustic system and lateral lemniscus) affected operant performance in rats across several auditory and visual reinforcement schedules. Lesions reduced lever-pressing and increased lever-releasing under auditory aversive schedules but produced no impairment in comparable visual conditions. Control manipulations of stimulus intensity or noise removal did not replicate the lesion effects, indicating that the auditory pathways play a distinct role in mediating aversive stimulus control rather than simple sensory detection or intensity modulation.

title: FREE-OPERANT BEHAVIOR UNDER CONDITIONS OF DELA YEDREINFORCEMENT. I. CRF-TYPE SCHEDULES
abstract: Pigeons were studied under continuous reinforcement–type schedules in which reinforcement followed a response after a fixed delay interval (10, 30, or 100 s). Response rates decreased with increasing delay but remained higher than those produced by noncontingent reinforcement at equivalent intervals, confirming that delayed reinforcement maintained operant control. Comparisons of schedule types revealed higher response rates when responses during the delay did not postpone reinforcement. Pharmacological tests showed that methamphetamine increased responding proportionally more at lower baseline rates, while pentobarbital enhanced rates more at higher baselines, suggesting delay-dependent modulation of drug effects.

title: THE ACQUISITION AND EXTINCTION OF CONDITIONED SUPPRESSIONAS A FUNCTION OF THE BASE-LINE REINFORCER
abstract: This study examined how the type of base-line reinforcer (sweetened milk vs. water) influences the acquisition and extinction of conditioned suppression in rats. Using a tone–shock pairing procedure, rats lever-pressed for either milk or water on a VI 2-min schedule. Suppression (reduction in responding during the conditioned stimulus) developed more slowly with milk reinforcement, suggesting stronger operant behavior under a more potent reinforcer. During extinction (shock omitted), suppression dissipated faster with milk than with water reinforcement. When reinforcers were switched between phases, suppression partially transferred, indicating that conditioned suppression was partly tied to the reinforcement context.

title: REPEATED CONDITIONING-EXTINCTION SESSIONS AS A FUNCTIONOF THE REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULE
static-equation-definitions: Response Units = extinction output expressed in reinforcement-schedule units (number of reinforcement-equivalent response clusters emitted during extinction); Total Extinction Responses = the number of responses emitted during the extinction period; Responses per Reinforcement = the reinforcement-schedule requirement (e.g., FR value or mean ratio/interval responses per reinforcer) used to normalize extinction output across schedules. Orientation note: the numerator/denominator ordering is inferred on dimensional and conceptual grounds (the response-unit measure of Mowrer & Jones, 1945, expresses extinction in units of the schedule's required response cluster, i.e., total responses divided by responses-per-reinforcement). The surviving corrupted fragment's literal token order points the opposite way, and the 1960 JEAB scan could not be machine-read, so the orientation rests on theory rather than direct confirmation against the page.
abstract: This study examined how different reinforcement schedules affect extinction performance in pigeons across repeated conditioning–extinction sessions. Three birds were trained on a fixed ratio (FR 10) and three on a fixed interval (FI 26 sec) schedule, each followed by a 60-minute extinction period. The number of extinction responses was converted to “response units” (responses per reinforcement) to compare schedules. Results showed that extinction responding stabilized within a narrow range, similar to findings in rats under comparable conditions (Weissman, 1959). Final extinction sessions were characterized by an initial “priming run” followed by pauses and occasional bursts, suggesting schedule-specific temporal control during extinction.

title: A semi-automatic teaching machine, 12
OPERANT DISCRIMINATION REVERSALS: COMPARA TIVE DA TA
process: Discrimination reversal learning and stimulus control
abstract: This comparative study examined discrimination reversal learning in a rat and a fish (Tilapia macrocephala) using a free-operant procedure with successive SD and SΔ presentations. Both species were trained to respond under a 30-second DRL contingency where illumination served as the discriminative stimulus. Over five reversals, both subjects showed decreasing SΔ responses, but the rat achieved reversal efficiency by the third reversal while the fish was still improving by the fifth. Further testing revealed that the rat’s responding came under control of the illumination change itself, rather than absolute intensity, indicating a shift in functional stimulus control across reversals.

title: SOME NOTES ON THE CONTROL OF CONDITIONED SUPPRESSION
abstract: Carlton and Didamo examined whether the rate or total number of reinforcements controls the degree of conditioned suppression in rats. Two subjects were trained to lever-press on a VI 2-minute schedule while periodic tones were paired with shock. The relative duration of tone (on-time/off-time) was varied across phases, with later phases delivering a constant total number of reinforcements. Suppression decreased as the proportion of tone time increased, despite total reinforcement being held constant—supporting the view that reinforcement rate, rather than total reinforcements missed, governs suppression. The authors proposed a discriminable “Weber–Fechner” type relationship between changes in reinforcement rate and suppression strength.

title: INTERMITTENT REINFORCEMENT OF MA TCHING TO SAMPLEIN THE PIGEON
process: Stimulus control and schedule-controlled matching behavior
static-equation-definitions: S^{D} = number (or rate) of responses to the correct, matching stimulus key; S^{\Delta} = number (or rate) of responses to the incorrect, non-matching stimulus key. The Accuracy Ratio expresses matching responses as a proportion of total responses (the standard proportion-correct measure). The Error Ratio expresses incorrect responses relative to correct responses. Note: both expressions are reconstructions from corrupted OCR fragments of a scanned (non-machine-readable) 1960 JEAB matching-to-sample paper, not a quantitative matching-law study; no canonical EAB model (Herrnstein/Baum/Davison-Tustin) applies. The numerator/denominator orientation of the Error Ratio is inferred on semantic grounds and is unverified: viable alternatives include S^{D}/S^{\Delta} (literal token order) and S^{\Delta}/(S^{D}+S^{\Delta}) (proportion of errors). These may be extraction-tool artifacts rather than formally displayed equations in the original.
abstract: Ferster extended the operant matching-to-sample paradigm to intermittent reinforcement schedules. Two pigeons were trained to peck a center key (sample) and then select one of two side keys (comparison) whose color either matched (SD) or did not match (SA) the sample. Matching responses produced brief conditioned reinforcers, while nonmatching responses produced short time-outs. The contingencies were arranged under fixed-ratio (FR), fixed-interval (FI), variable-interval (VI), and multiple FI–FR schedules. Matching accuracy increased with moderate ratio sizes (peaking at FR 15–20) and declined when ratios became too large (“ratio strain”). SA (nonmatching) responses were higher under interval schedules than ratio schedules. The findings demonstrated that complex chained discriminations could display the same schedule-controlled response patterns as simple operants, supporting the generality of reinforcement-schedule principles.

title: TEACHING MA CHINES: AN APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLESFROM THE LABORATORY
process: Programmed instruction and operant shaping of verbal behavior

abstract: Holland outlines the conceptual foundation of teaching machines as an application of operant conditioning principles rather than a mechanical innovation. He emphasizes that the essential advance lies in using reinforcement-based behavioral engineering to shape learning systematically, not in the hardware itself. Teaching machines automate the presentation of finely sequenced tasks and immediate feedback to ensure steady progress and individualized pacing. Data from revisions of a Harvard psychology program demonstrated that improvements in programmed material—based on student performance analyses—halved error rates and completion times. Holland concludes that genuine progress in education depends on applying experimentally derived behavioral principles, not mere automation.

title: WA TER-DEPRIVA TION-PRODUCED SIGN REVERSAL OF ACONDITIONED REINFORCER BASED UPON DRY FOOD'
abstract: Pliskoff and Tolliver (1960) demonstrated that a conditioned reinforcer established through correlation with dry-food reinforcement can reverse its behavioral function under water deprivation. Rats performed on a fixed-ratio food lever and a timeout (TO) lever that produced a 5-minute suspension of food availability signaled by light and tone. Under normal conditions, TOs were rare, but during water deprivation, rats increasingly initiated TOs, suggesting that the stimuli previously associated with food (the TO complex) acquired aversive properties. When the TO contingency was placed on extinction, responding extinguished, confirming that the TO served as a negative reinforcer under thirst.

title: SOME ELECTRONIC CONTROL UNITS FOR OPERANT BEHAVIOR STUDIES:III. A TIMER AND COUNTER WITH PRINT-OUT
authors: Schoenfiled, W.N.; Cumming, W.W.; Hearst, E.; Waine, M.; Snapper, A.G.; Haas, P.
process: Measurement and control technology in operant conditioning
abstract: Schoenfeld, Cumming, Snapper, and Haas (1960) describe an electronic timing and counting apparatus designed for operant behavior research. The device measures response durations, interresponse times, and event frequencies over programmable intervals, with automated printout via a Hewlett-Packard digital recorder. It can resolve inter-event intervals as brief as 10 microseconds and durations down to 1 millisecond, offering adjustable accuracy through selectable tone frequencies (1 kHz–10 kHz). The unit integrates counting, timing, and signal coding functions to support diverse experimental contingencies in operant analysis.

title: SINGLE AND MULTIPLE SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT INDEVELOPMENTALLY RETARDED CHILDREN'
abstract: Orlando and Bijou (1960) examined operant performance under single and multiple schedules of reinforcement in 46 institutionalized developmentally retarded children. Using candy reinforcers and free-operant lever pressing, the study analyzed response patterns under variable interval (VI), fixed interval (FI), variable ratio (VR), and fixed ratio (FR) schedules, as well as multiple VR–extinction and CRF–extinction schedules. The findings showed that the children’s response rates, pause distributions, and discrimination behaviors followed the same general patterns as those reported for nonhuman subjects, demonstrating reliable schedule control and stable responding under both simple and multiple contingencies.

title: SOME SCHEDULES INVOLVING A VERSIVE CONTROL"
process: Aversive control and stimulus control in operant discrimination
abstract: Appel (1960) studied monkeys on aversive multiple and mixed schedules combining Sidman avoidance (response postpones shock) with punishment (response produces shock) or extinction. Using discriminative stimuli (lights/noise) and reversals, he showed monkeys reliably discriminate avoidance vs. punishment (high rates in avoidance, near-zero in punishment), but discrimination between avoidance and extinction required distinct external stimuli. Adding unavoidable “free” shocks during extinction elevated response rates in both components.

title: SOME OBSERVATIONS CONCERNING PREPOTENCY AND PROBABILITY OFPOSTPONING SHOCK WITH A TWO-LEVER AVOIDANCE PROCEDURE
process: Free-operant avoidance with concurrent options; choice/response allocation under aversive control.
abstract: Verhave used a two-lever free-operant avoidance setup in rats to study how response allocation (“prepotency”) depends on the probability that a lever press postpones shock (P). With both levers equally effective (PA = PB = 100%), animals often developed dominance on one lever but also exhibited abrupt within- and between-session switching. When probabilities were made unequal (e.g., PA < PB), responding shifted—sometimes gradually, sometimes abruptly—toward the lever with the higher P. After stabilization, rats tended to “play it safe,” responding almost exclusively on the higher-probability lever; the ratio of lever rates did not track the ratio of P values.

title: SCHEDULES OF CONDITIONED REINFORCEMENT DURINGEXPERIMENTAL EXTINCTION
process: Conditioned reinforcement and schedule control of operant behavior during extinction.
abstract: Kelleher (1960) examined the effects of conditioned reinforcement during extinction by using the sound of a food magazine as a reinforcer for pigeons previously trained on an FI 5-minute food schedule. During extinction, food was withheld but the magazine sound was delivered on differential reinforcement of pausing (DRP), fixed interval (FI), or fixed ratio (FR) schedules. Distinct response patterns emerged under each condition: low rates under DRP, scalloped FI patterns under FI schedules, and high steady rates under FR schedules—demonstrating that the magazine sound functioned as a conditioned reinforcer capable of maintaining schedule-typical behavior in the absence of primary reinforcement.

title: RAPID DEVELOPMENT OF MULTIPLE-SCHEDULE PERFORMANCESWITH RETARDED CHILDREN
process: Acquisition of discriminated operant behavior and multiple-schedule performance through shaping and reinforcement
abstract: Bijou and Orlando (1960) outlined an efficient method for establishing multiple-schedule performance in institutionalized developmentally retarded children. The study described a systematic shaping procedure—using brief, simple instructions and edible reinforcers—to transition children from initial lever-pressing behavior to discriminated responding under alternating reinforcement and extinction components. The technique allowed subjects to progress at their own pace and demonstrated that complex schedule control (e.g., mult FR 25 ext, mult FI 1 ext, mult CRF VI 0.5) could be achieved within a few sessions rather than weeks, offering a rapid approach for studying discrimination and individual variability in human operant conditioning.

title: A VOIDANCE LEARNING IN DOGS WITHOUT AWARNING STIMULUS'
process: avoidance learning and maintenance; effects of punishment and psychostimulant
abstract: Black and Morse (1960) demonstrated that dogs can acquire and maintain avoidance responding in the absence of a warning stimulus using a shuttle-box jumping operant. Acquisition was highly sensitive to the temporal parameters of shock delivery: dogs learned rapidly at short shock–shock (S–S) intervals (0–4 s) but failed to acquire avoidance at longer intervals (15 s). Once established, the behavior was stable and maintained with minimal shock. Subsequent manipulations showed that punishment initially increased responding before producing suppression, with the duration of this effect depending on prior training. Amphetamine produced dose-dependent rate increases and disrupted punishment discrimination at high doses.

title: THE CONTROL OF THE CONTENT OF CONVERSATIONTHROUGH REINFORCEMENT
authors: Azrin, N.H.; Holz, W.; Ulrich, R.; Goldiamond, I.
abstract: Azrin, Holz, Ulrich, and Goldiamond (1960) attempted to replicate Verplanck’s (1955) finding that conversation content could be modified by reinforcement—specifically, that agreement with opinions increases their frequency. Across several classroom replications with graduate and undergraduate students, the authors found apparent effects of reinforcement, but also major procedural inconsistencies, poor reliability in identifying “opinions,” and even fabricated data. A final replication by trained psychologists failed entirely: when reinforcement (agreement/disagreement) was systematically limited, subjects quickly terminated the conversation. The study highlights methodological challenges in extending operant conditioning to uncontrolled verbal behavior and stresses the necessity of objective recording and response definition.

title: THE SHAPE OF SOME WA VELENGTH GENERA LIZA TION GRA DIEN T
abstract: Blough (1961) examined the shape and shifts of wavelength generalization gradients in pigeons trained to peck a key illuminated by specific monochromatic lights (530, 550, or 570 mµ). Following reinforcement at one wavelength and testing in extinction across a range (490–610 mµ), pigeons produced reproducible, wavelength-centered gradients that shifted appropriately when training wavelength changed. Gradient forms varied across birds and wavelengths—some symmetrical, others asymmetrical—suggesting spectral regions where generalization occurs more readily (e.g., around 570 mµ). The findings challenge assumptions linking gradient steepness with discriminability and indicate that generalization patterns may reveal aspects of avian color perception.

title: AMPLITUDE-INDUCTION GRADIENT OF A SMALL HUMAN OPERANTIN A N ESCA PE-A VOIDA NCE SITUA TION
process: Response induction (amplitude differentiation) within operant conditioning
abstract: Hefferline and Keenan (1960) analyzed the amplitude-induction gradient of a small electromyographically recorded thumb-contraction operant in a human escape–avoidance setting. The subject, unaware of the specific response, learned to terminate or postpone an aversive noise by producing microvolt-level muscle contractions. Reinforcement of a specific amplitude range induced increased responding in adjacent amplitude subclasses, forming an induction gradient analogous to a stimulus generalization gradient. Larger amplitudes appeared briefly then declined, while responses near the reinforced amplitude persisted until extinction. The findings demonstrate fine-grained response differentiation and operant induction in human microbehavior.

title: PUNISHMENT OF SA RESPONDING IN MATCHING TO SAMPLEBY TIME OUT FROM POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT'"
process: Punishment by time out from positive reinforcement
abstract: Ferster and Appel (1961) examined how time out (TO) from positive reinforcement functions as punishment for incorrect (SΔ) responses in a pigeon matching-to-sample task. Two pigeons were trained under continuous (CRF) and variable-interval (VI 3-min) reinforcement schedules while TO durations ranged from 0.5 to 600 seconds. Under CRF, long TOs (up to 10 minutes) produced little suppression, but under VI 3-min schedules, moderate TO durations (10–60 s) maximally increased matching accuracy by selectively suppressing SΔ responding without broadly reducing overall response rate. Very long TOs (≥120 s) disrupted performance entirely. The results show that the punishing effectiveness of time out depends on both its duration and the reinforcement schedule maintaining the behavior.

title: BEHA VIORAL CONTRAST
abstract: Reynolds (1961) investigated behavioral contrast—the change in response rate to one stimulus when the reinforcement schedule associated with another stimulus is altered. Pigeons responded on a multiple schedule in which key color (e.g., red vs. green) signaled different reinforcement contingencies. When reinforcement during one component was replaced by extinction or time-out, response rates during the unchanged component increased (positive contrast). However, when non-responding during the alternate component was itself reinforced (DRO), the contrast effect disappeared, showing that contrast depends on relative reinforcement frequency rather than response suppression alone. The findings supported a relativistic interpretation of contrast: the rate of responding in a given condition depends on the relative frequency of reinforcement across all concurrently alternating conditions.

CONDITIONING OF MENTAL-HOSPITAL PATIENTS TO FIXED-RATIOSCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT'
abstract: Hutchinson and Azrin (1960) studied the acquisition and maintenance of operant responding under fixed-ratio (FR) reinforcement schedules in five long-term hospitalized patients diagnosed with schizophrenia. Using cigarettes or candy as reinforcers, patients pulled a manipulandum to earn rewards under progressively increasing FR requirements. Response rates began extremely low (≈5/min) but gradually increased over sessions, reaching >100/min at higher ratios (up to FR 300). Performances showed the characteristic pause-run pattern typical of FR schedules, with pauses localized after reinforcement. When ratio requirements were increased too rapidly (“ratio strain”), performance temporarily deteriorated but recovered with lower ratios. Extinction produced alternating bouts of high-rate responding and pausing until responding ceased. Conditioned reinforcers (light + buzzer) reinstated responding after primary reinforcement was withdrawn. Despite psychiatric diagnosis, the behavioral patterns closely resembled those of nonclinical human and animal subjects.

process: Extinction effects on temporal structure and sequencing of an operant chain
abstract: "A 10-year-old horse was conditioned to nudge a lever with its snout to receive small grain reinforcers. After shaping under continuous reinforcement, the animal was exposed to fixed-ratio (FR 3–11) and fixed-interval (FI 1–3 min) schedules. The horse qui

title: AN ANALYSIS OF INTERACTIONS IN A MULTIPLE SCHEDULE
abstract: Reynolds (1961) analyzed how components of two-stimulus multiple schedules interact in pigeons. In daily 3-h sessions (30 cycles of 3-min components), birds experienced sequences combining VI 3-min or VR 150:1 with EXT. Rates in a component held on reinforcement increased when the alternated component switched to EXT (behavioral contrast) and decreased when it switched to reinforcement. In an EXT component, switching the other component to EXT reduced responding (negative induction) whereas switching it to reinforcement produced a transient increase (positive induction). Extinction in one component was slower when alternated with VI (but not VR), consistent with VI-generated pausing functioning as a discriminative stimulus. During discrimination formation after EXT-EXT, induced responding depended on prior history: reversal (VI→EXT) > formation (VI→VI) > re-formation (EXT→VI).

title: VISUAL EXPLORATION AS REINFORCEMENT OF CONDITIONEDBAR-PRESSING RESPONSES OF MONKEYS
abstract: "Moon (1960) demonstrated that visual exploration—allowing monkeys to view their surroundings through a briefly opened window—can serve as an effective reinforcer for bar-pressing behavior. Thirteen rhesus monkeys were tested under FR, VI, and DRL schedules. The animals maintained high and stable response rates without the need for food or water deprivation, and exhibited minimal satiation across sessions. When permitted to control the window duration, monkeys spent roughly 50–60% of the session exploring visually. The study proposed visual exploration as a practical and ethologically relevant reinforcer, especially useful in psychopharmacological contexts."]

title: A MO UNT OF REINFORCEMENT A ND FREE-OPERA NT RESPONDING
abstract: Keesey and Kling (1961) investigated how varying the amount of food reinforcement affects free-operant responding in pigeons. Across variable-interval schedules, pigeons were exposed to different food quantities (¼, 1, 2, 3, and 4 peas) each paired with a unique key color. Once stable performance was achieved, response rates did not systematically differ by reinforcement amount. However, transient differences appeared early in sessions, during extinction, or immediately following procedural changes, suggesting that response rate sensitivity to reinforcement amount emerges when steady-state behavior is disrupted. The authors proposed that extensive exposure leads to a generalized conditioned reinforcement value that overrides differences in amount.

title: RESISTANCE-TO-EXTINCTION FUNCTIONS IN THE SINGLE ORGANISM
process: Operant extinction and resistance to extinction
abstract: Hearst (1961) measured resistance to extinction within individual pigeons by pairing four key colors with different reinforcement histories, then testing all colors in extinction. In Experiment I, total extinction responses and response probability increased (negatively accelerated at the group level) with the number of prior reinforcements, though individuals showed idiosyncratic gradients. In Experiment II, the extinction responding was an increasing function of the conditioning variable ratio (VR 1, 4, 10), reproducing the partial-reinforcement effect within subjects. The method yields both individual and group resistance-to-extinction functions without separate groups.
