STIMULUS GENERALIZATION IN AN AVOIDANCE SITUATION
process: Stimulus generalization and discrimination in free-operant (Sidman) avoidance.
abstract: Sidman measured stimulus generalization of free-operant avoidance in two rhesus monkeys. After discrimination training (avoidance with 2 Hz clicks vs. extinction with 6 Hz), he probed a series of click rates (≈2–6 Hz). Generalization gradients (percent of total responding per stimulus) were orderly and usually centered near the training S+; switching the “anchor” stimulus and prolonged testing could sharpen the gradient. Manipulating response–shock intervals and shock duration scaled overall response rates but left the gradient’s shape largely unchanged. A “generalization surface” showed a roughly linear relation between per-stimulus rate and session-wide rate, with slopes decreasing as stimuli diverged from S+.

title: OPERANT CONTROL OF VOCALIZING IN THE CHICKEN
abstract: Lane demonstrated operant control of vocal behavior in Bantam chicks. Chirping was reinforced under fixed-ratio, fixed-interval, differential-reinforcement-of-other-behavior (DRO), and multiple schedules. Rates of vocalizing conformed to standard operant patterns (e.g., post-reinforcement pauses, scalloping, extinction decline). Discriminative control developed under multiple FI–EXT schedules, and differential responding persisted after reversal. Concurrent and conjunctive schedules involving chirping and pecking revealed both functional independence and interactions between the two operants. Overall, the study confirmed that vocalization in chickens can be governed by contingencies of reinforcement like other operant responses.

title: RELATIVITY OF RESPONSE RATE AND REINFORCEMENTFREQUENCY IN A MULTIPLE SCHEDULE
process: Behavioral contrast and relative rate of responding as a function of relative reinforcement frequency (precursor to the Matching Law)
static-equation-definitions: R_c = relative rate of responding in component c (response rate in component c divided by the total response rate across components of the multiple schedule); F_c = relative frequency of reinforcement in component c (reinforcements in component c divided by total reinforcements across components); 0.13 (intercept) and 0.8 (slope) are the fitted coefficients of a linear relation between relative response rate and relative reinforcement frequency, reported as extracted from the fragment. Fit method is not verifiable from the scanned-only source (the "least-squares regression" attribution is not asserted as fact). This empirical near-matching line (slope < 1, small positive intercept, i.e. undermatching-like deviation from strict equality) is the central relation of Reynolds (1961) and a direct precursor to Herrnstein's (1961) relative-rate matching law R_1/(R_1+R_2) = r_1/(r_1+r_2).
abstract: Reynolds examined how pigeons’ response rates in one component of a multiple schedule depend on the relative frequency of reinforcement across components. Using VI–FR multiple schedules, he showed that as the relative reinforcement frequency for a constant component increased, the response rate in that component rose proportionally—even when its absolute reinforcement rate was unchanged. Across both VI–FR and FR–VI arrangements, the relative response rate closely approximated a linear function of the relative reinforcement frequency, with slope ≈ 0.8 and intercept ≈ 0.13. The study refined the concept of behavioral contrast as part of a broader law of relative reinforcement.

title: A variable probability coincidence pulse gate
SEPARATION OF TWO- CHANNEL RECORDINGS FORVOCAL BEHAVIOR STUDIES
process: Technological facilitation of verbal behavior measurement
abstract: Starkweather and Langsley described a two-channel switching system designed to eliminate crosstalk in simultaneous recordings of two people’s voices during social or clinical interactions. Using voice-activated keys (modified Heathkit VX-1 circuits) that alternately silence the opposite channel through diode-modulated relay circuits, each person’s voice could be recorded cleanly without interference from the other. The apparatus permitted later playback for automatic voice-duration and rate analyses and could generate clean separated tapes suitable for linguistic or behavioral research.

title: A METHOD FOR THE ANALYSIS AND CONTROL OFSPEECH RATE'
authors: Shearn, D.; Sprague, R.; Rosenzweig, S.
process: Operant conditioning of verbal response rate
abstract: Shearn, Sprague, and Rosenzweig (1961) developed an operant method for quantifying and controlling speech rate using an electronic voice-control manipulandum (a modified Heathkit VX-1 voice key). College students produced vocal responses reinforced on fixed-ratio (FR 30) schedules, while a psychiatric patient received contingent reinforcement on differential-reinforcement-of-low-rate (DRL) schedules. The apparatus transformed speech bursts into discrete measurable responses, allowing automated contingency control. Under FR schedules, speech rate increased and showed extinction patterns; under DRL schedules, the patient’s speech rate progressively decreased as interval requirements lengthened, demonstrating operant control of verbal response pacing.

title: A TTENTION IN THE PIGEON
abstract: Reynolds (1961) studied selective attention in pigeons using compound visual stimuli. In Experiment 1, pecks were reinforced to a triangle-on-red and extinguished to a circle-on-green; when elements were tested separately, one pigeon responded to shape (triangle) while the other responded to color (red), showing control by only one component of the compound. In Experiment 2, a side-lamp signaled which element would be reinforced (color vs. shape). Despite wavelength changes, behavior tracked the presence/intensity of the side-lamp rather than its hue, indicating stimulus control by intensity and not the nominal signaling dimension. Overall, the work demonstrates that pigeons may attend to a single effective aspect of a compound discriminative stimulus.

title: THE USE OF A BEHA VIORA L STIMULANT INTHE STUDY OF STIMULUS GENERALIZATION
abstract: Hanson and Guttman (1961) examined the effects of the behavioral stimulant pipradrol on stimulus generalization gradients in pigeons trained to peck a key illuminated at 550 nm. After VI training, birds received extinction generalization tests with wavelengths ranging from 490–640 nm. Experimental pigeons received 8 mg/kg pipradrol prior to testing, controls received saline. The stimulant markedly reduced extinction (sustaining response rate across tests) but did not alter the shape or spread of generalization gradients. Thus, pipradrol increased general activity while leaving the underlying stimulus control by wavelength unchanged.

title: SEPTAL STIMULATION AS A REINFORCER OF AND AN ALTERNATIVETO CONSUMA TORY BEHA VIOR
process: Intracranial self-stimulation as operant reinforcement and its interaction/competition with consummatory (drinking) behavior.
abstract: Falk (1961) investigated whether septal-area intracranial stimulation (ICS) could serve as a reinforcer for or alternative to water consumption in rats. Two female rats with electrodes in the medial septal nucleus were tested under various conditions combining lever-press–elicited ICS and drinkometer-activated water access. While ICS effectively reinforced lever pressing, it did not increase water intake when made contingent on licking. At higher stimulation voltages, rats even chose ICS over drinking despite prolonged water deprivation, resuming drinking only after severe dehydration. Thus, septal stimulation acted as a potent competing reinforcer rather than one that potentiated consummatory behavior.

title: SPACED RESPONDING IN RATS AS A FUNCTION OF SOME TEMPORAL VARIABLES
process: Schedule control of temporal spacing (DRL timing/temporal discrimination) via reinforcement-rate consequences.
abstract: Zimmerman compared two discrete-trial DRL arrangements that differed in how response timing affected reinforcement rate. In the recycling DRL, each response (reinforced or not) produced a 6-s SΔ and immediately started a new trial, so tighter spacing after reinforcement setup could raise reinforcement rate. In the fixed-trial DRL, the trial length was fixed; spacing after setup could not change reinforcement rate. With DRL 18-s LH 12 and DRL 6-s LH 24, recycling yielded shorter, more peaked SD→response (SD-R) distributions than fixed-trial; with DRL 6-s LH 2 (short limited hold), the schedules produced similar timing. Conclusion: reinforcement-rate consequences strongly shape spaced responding, though an additional factor promotes clustering near the first reinforced bin even when rate consequences are removed.

title: DISCRIMINATIVE PROPERTIES OF PUNISHMENT
process: Discriminative control (stimulus control) via punishment contingencies; interaction between aversive and discriminative functions of stimuli.
abstract: Holz and Azrin (1961) examined how punishment can acquire discriminative control over responding in pigeons. Pigeons pecked under variable-interval reinforcement schedules in which electric shock (punishment) was paired either with reinforcement or with extinction. When shock was consistently paired with reinforcement, punishment increased responding—even in extinction. Conversely, when a mild, nonaversive shock was paired with extinction, its later presentation decreased responding. Thus, punishment’s effect depended on its differential association with reinforcement or extinction, revealing that punishment can function as a discriminative stimulus rather than solely as an aversive consequence.

title: A N OPERA NT-DISCRIMINA TION A PPA RA TUS FOR INFANTS
process: Operant discrimination and reinforcement learning in human infants.
abstract: Simmons and Lipsitt (1961) designed an automated operant discrimination apparatus for infants, enabling the study of learning and sensory discrimination before the onset of speech. Infants interacted with two manipulanda (panels) that could be lit in different colors and accompanied by auditory reinforcement (e.g., chimes). By alternately pairing one panel with reinforcement and the other without, the authors demonstrated that 10- to 12-month-old infants could learn simple color–sound discriminations and adjust responding when contingencies were reversed. The apparatus allows quantitative analysis of early operant and discriminative behavior.

title: GENERALIZATION OF AUDITORY INTENSITY AS A FUNCTION OFAMOUNT OF DISCRIMINATION TRAINING
abstract: "Sherman & Pierrel (1961) trained rats on an auditory intensity discrimination (SD vs. a louder SA) for different durations (6, 13, 27 days), then tested generalization across multiple attenuated intensities. Longer prior discrimination produced sharper, smoother generalization gradients with lower variability; gradients steepened further with continued multi-SA training, approaching asymptote within ~10 days.

title: INFLUENCE OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES ON RESPONSE DURATION'
process: Operant temporal topography (response duration) under schedule control; schedule effects (FI
and probability-based contingencies) on response variability.
abstract: Millenson, Hurwitz, & Nixon (1961) examined how reinforcement schedules shape lever-press response duration in rats. Compared to CRF, fixed-interval (FI) schedules produced longer, more variable, positively skewed duration distributions; extended exposure to FI yielded modest, inconsistent trends. Under contingencies approximating uniform reinforcement probability (T = proportion of time reinforcement available), both median duration and dispersion peaked around T ≈ 0.11. With FR 5, durations were short with narrow dispersion and asymmetric distributions, and showed no consistent within-ratio (1st–5th press) differences.

title: SOME BEHAVIORAL EFFECTS OF A CONCURRENTLY POSITIVEAND NEGATIVE STIMULUS
abstract: Hearst & Sidman studied rats pressing one lever that produced both food (VI) and shock (FR)—a concurrently positive–negative (reward–punishment) situation—with a second “escape” lever that switched to a neutral timeout (no food, no shock). About half the rats learned reliable escape only when both reward and punishment co-occurred; removing either contingency greatly reduced escape. Others instead adopted low, steady rates on the food/shock lever and rarely escaped. In a variant where escape also reset the shock counter, escape responding increased sharply. Results suggest it’s the combination of appetitive and aversive consequences—not either alone—that drives escape from the discriminative context.

authors: Heferline, R.F.; Birch, J.D.; Gentry, T.

process: Schedule interaction and induction between timing (DRL) and variable-interval responding
abstract: "Azrin, Holz, Ulrich, and Goldiamond (1960) attempted to replicate Verplanck’s (1955) finding that conversation content could be modified by reinforcement—specifically, that agreement with opinions increases their frequency. Across several classroom repli

title: RELATIVE AND ABSOLUTE. STRENGTH OF RESPONSE AS A FUNCTIONOF FREQUENCY OF REINFORCEMENT
process: Concurrent schedule performance — matching law and response strength as functions of reinforcement frequency.
static-equation-definitions: $p$, $p_1$, $p_2$ = frequency (number) of responses, generic and on alternatives 1 and 2 of a concurrent schedule; $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$ = frequency of reinforcement, generic and on alternatives 1 and 2; $k$ = constant of proportionality. Eq. 1 expresses the "absolute" view that response strength is proportional to its own frequency of reinforcement; Eq. 2 is Herrnstein's matching law: relative response frequency equals relative reinforcement frequency. The two cohere mathematically, since applying $p_i = k e_i$ per alternative yields $p_1/(p_1+p_2) = e_1/(e_1+e_2)$.

abstract: "Bijou and Orlando (1960) outlined an efficient method for establishing multiple-schedule performance in institutionalized developmentally retarded children. The study described a systematic shaping procedure—using brief, simple instructions and edible re

title: FREE-OPERANT A VOIDANCE CONDITIONING IN HUMAN SUBJECTS
process: Free-operant (Sidman) avoidance conditioning — maintenance of behavior by postponement of an aversive event without external warning stimuli.
abstract: "Bijou and Orlando (1960) outlined an efficient method for establishing multiple-schedule performance in institutionalized developmentally retarded children. The study described a systematic shaping procedure—using brief, simple instructions and edible re

title: DISCRETE-TRIALS DRL
abstract: "Logan (1961) examined discrete-trials differential reinforcement of low rate (DRL) schedules to compare bar-pressing performance in an operant chamber with alley-running behavior under negatively correlated reinforcement. Four rats were trained to delay bar pressing following a light signal to receive food. The procedure produced unimodal response-time distributions similar to alley performance, with few short latencies but more excessively long ones. The study demonstrated that discrete-trials DRL eliminated rapid responses common in free-operant DRL and suggested that spatial orientation at trial onset influences timing precision."]

title: SOME DATA ON MATCHING BEHAVIOR IN THE PIGEON
process: Conditional discrimination (matching-to-sample behavior) and stimulus control acquisition.
abstract: Cumming and Berryman (1961) studied color matching behavior in pigeons using a three-key apparatus. Each trial began with illumination of a center key (red, green, or blue) followed by two comparison keys—one matching and one nonmatching in hue. A peck on the matching key produced reinforcement, while the nonmatching choice produced a blackout. Pigeons rapidly acquired accurate matching performance after several sessions, progressing from position-based responding to color-controlled matching. When a novel yellow stimulus was introduced, pigeons reverted to position preferences, indicating the absence of generalized “matching-to-sample” concept formation.

title: Techniques of housing and maintaining a large pigeon colony1
SOME EFFECTS OF VARYING THE DURATION OF AN EXTEROCEPTIVEWARNING STIMULUS ON INTERCURRENT AVOIDANCE ANDA PPETITIVE RESPONSES
process: reconditioning effects and stimulus generalization involving variations in the conditioned stimulus duration.
abstract: Halasz (1961) investigated how changes in the duration of a conditioned warning stimulus (CS) affect intercurrent avoidance and appetitive behavior in a cat trained to both press a lever for milk and deflect a pendulum to avoid shock. After stable avoidance and food-maintained responding were established, the CS was shortened and terminated by the experimenter, weakening avoidance. When the original long CS duration was restored (without shock), the avoidance response reappeared strongly, producing renewed after-suppression of appetitive responding. The findings suggest second-order reconditioning of avoidance via CS duration and highlight stimulus generalization and induction processes in avoidance maintenance.

title: CONTRAST, GENERALIZATION, AND THE PROCESSOF DISCRIMINATION
process: Stimulus control & generalization under discrimination training; behavioral contrast; peak-shift phenomena.
abstract: "Blough (1961) examined the shape and shifts of wavelength generalization gradients in pigeons trained to peck a key illuminated by specific monochromatic lights (530, 550, or 570 mµ). Following reinforcement at one wavelength and testing in extinction ac

title: EXTINCTION OF BAR PRESSING FOLLOWING TRAININGUNDER A MULTIPLE VI VI SCHEDULE
process: Multiple-schedule performance and extinction dynamics (differential response persistence across variable-interval components).
abstract: Four albino rats were trained to press a bar under a multiple VI 15 s / VI 75 s schedule with alternating noise stimuli. Two rats were later extinguished under identical stimulus durations, and two under equalized durations. For the “same” (S) group, response rates remained higher under the VI 15 s condition, showing an accentuated rate ratio during extinction. For the “different” (D) group, equalized stimulus durations produced either no change or a slight decrease in rate ratio. Results suggest that interaction effects between VI components contribute to differential extinction patterns beyond simple duration effects.

title: A SIMPLE NOISE SOURCE
abstract: This paper describes a simple electronic circuit for generating audio noise with random spectral characteristics. The design uses only four components and produces output with approximately equal energy per octave across the audio spectrum. The circuit can function either as a low-level noise source for microphone preamplifiers or, with an added amplifier stage, as a higher-output source suitable for driving audio amplifier inputs.

title: THE DIFFERENTIATION OF HUMAN TIME ESTIMATIONS'
authors: Taber, J.I.; Homme, L.E.; Csanyi, A.
process: Temporal differentiation (operant timing / differential reinforcement of response duration).
abstract: This study examined how humans learn to estimate time intervals through differential reinforcement of a “holding” response, analogous to operant timing in animals. Using a mechanical ergograph and feedback lights, subjects learned to hold a lever for a specified interval (e.g., 1 second) to receive reinforcement. In Experiment I, untrained human estimations became highly precise after differential reinforcement, with variability reduced sixfold. In Experiment II, time intervals ranging from 0.5 to 5 seconds were tested, showing that relative variability decreased as the interval length increased, approximating Weber’s law. The findings suggest that human timing behavior, though initially variable, can be systematically shaped through reinforcement.

title: THE INFLUENCE OF REPETITION OF INCORRECTLY ANSWEREDITEMS IN A TEACHING-MACHINE PROGRAM1
process: Programmed instruction / differential reinforcement via immediate feedback and required correct responding (error correction)
abstract: Graduate students worked through a programmed instruction course either with item-by-item review (missed items re-presented until correct) or without review (each item seen once). On three immediate tests, the review group made fewer errors at all difficulty levels (≈4–13 percentage-point advantage). On an unannounced retest 6 months later, both groups showed forgetting, larger for harder items, but the review group remained superior. Review cost ~1.3 extra minutes per 29-item set (~1.3 hours total across 60 sets). Authors argue repetition of missed items materially improves acquisition and long-term retention when error rates are nontrivial.

title: A simple shock circuit for rats1
DISCRIMINATED BAR-PRESS AVOIDANCE
authors: Hoffman, H.S.; Fleshler, M.; Chorny, H.
abstract: Rats learned signaled (tone) bar-press avoidance of shock. Over ~50 sessions, some reached ≥90% avoidance, while others persistently showed within-session “warm-up” (poor early, good late performance). Follow-ups varied shock intensity, removed the warning tone for initial trials, and blocked bar access during unsignaled shocks. Raising shock intensity didn’t fix deficits; eliminating the tone or preventing the response still abolished warm-up. Authors conclude warm-up reflects a shock-induced motivational/emotional process rather than sensitivity to shock, relearning of tone–shock, or response execution per se.

title: RESPONSE DURATION IN OPERANT LEVEL,REGULAR REIANFORCEMENT, AND EXTINCTION
process: Operant conditioning with continuous reinforcement and subsequent extinction
abstract: Rats’ bar-press duration was measured across operant level (baseline), continuous reinforcement, and extinction. Mean duration was long at baseline, shortened and stabilized under regular reinforcement (more short presses; narrower range), then lengthened again through extinction (with within-session increases and spontaneous recovery). Duration distributions late in conditioning resembled early-extinction distributions; late-extinction resembled operant level. More conditioning reinforcers produced a higher fraction of short-duration presses in both conditioning and extinction, and greater resistance to extinction.

title: A coupled tape programmer and buffer box1
THE DEVELOPMENT OF AN INSTRUMENTAL SKILL SEQUENCEIN THE CHIMPANZEE
process: Acquisition and maintenance of a discrimination-based instrumental chain under fixed-ratio reinforcement
abstract: A chimpanzee was trained to press one of three levers corresponding to the “odd” visual stimulus (circle, triangle, or square). Over repeated sessions, accuracy increased from chance to ~99%. Once stable, the schedule was shifted from continuous reinforcement (CRF) to fixed ratio (FR), progressing up to FR-19. Both discrimination accuracy and response rate increased with higher ratios. The chimp eventually appeared to perform the 18-set discrimination sequence as a learned serial chain, suggesting acquisition of a complex instrumental skill.

title: A liquid dispenser for primates
TIMING BEHAVIOR DURING PROLONGED TREATMENT WITH dl-AMPHETAMINE
abstract: Rats trained on a differential reinforcement of low rates (DRL 17.5 s) schedule received chronic intraperitoneal injections of dl-amphetamine (0.75–1.5 mg/kg). Initially, amphetamine produced typical stimulant effects—shortened interresponse times (IRTs), increased response rates, and reduced reinforcement. Over repeated sessions, however, performance gradually returned toward baseline despite continued drug exposure, indicating behavioral tolerance specific to the operant task. In contrast, general locomotor activity remained elevated throughout, suggesting differential tolerance across behavioral systems.

title: A bidirectional cumulative recorder1
An automatic feeder for laboratory dogs1
BEHAVIORAL CONTRAST IN A MULTIPLE AND CONCURRENTSCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Pigeons pecked two keys under combined multiple–concurrent schedules. When a VI component (green) on one “multiple” key alternated with extinction (yellow), response rate in the VI component increased—behavioral contrast. Crucially, if the overall reinforcement rate during the extinction components was restored (by arranging reinforcement on the other, concurrent key while the multiple key was in extinction), the contrast vanished. Across manipulations, the magnitude of contrast scaled with the relative drop in reinforcement rate during extinction. Local performance analyses showed higher overall VI rates emerged largely from shorter cycles (reduced changeover and red-key run times), with only minor changes in within-run rates on the VI key.

title: PUNISHMENT DURING FIXED-INTERVAL REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Two pigeons pecked under FI 5-min food reinforcement while every response was punished with brief tail shock (30–180 V). Punishment always reduced overall responding; mild intensities showed partial recovery across days, stronger intensities produced sustained suppression. The within-interval pattern (low post-reinforcement rate rising to a high terminal rate) was proportionally depressed across the entire FI, leaving the temporal pattern essentially unchanged (confirmed via Quarter-life and Curvature indices). During extinction with punishment still present, higher shock intensities yielded fewer responses and much faster cessation.

title: COLLATERAL BEHAVIOR IN HUMANS'
process: Collateral behavior and conditioned reinforcement processes emerging under DRL schedules
abstract: Four high school students pressed telegraph keys under a DRL (Differential Reinforcement of Low Rates) schedule, where reinforcement occurred only if the interval between presses on one designated key was between 8.2 s and 10.25 s. The other three keys had no programmed consequence but allowed observation of collateral behavior. Each participant developed stable, idiosyncratic sequences of presses on the nonreinforced keys that filled the waiting interval before reinforcement. During extinction, these organized chains disappeared. Subjects often believed reinforcement depended on particular key sequences rather than timing.

title: EFFECTS OF CHRONICALLY ADMINISTERED CHLORPROMAZINEON MULTIPLE-SCHEDULE PERFORMANCE1
process: Drug effects on discriminative control under multiple schedules
abstract: Two beagle dogs were trained on multiple schedules (FI 3-min, FR 50, and SΔ 25-min components) and given chronic daily oral doses of chlorpromazine in sustained-release (spansule) form (1–24 mg/kg). Low doses increased responding in both interval and ratio components, suggesting reduced stimulus control and increased induction between components. Higher doses produced rate depression, erratic responding, or intermittent bursts, yet substantial behavior persisted even at 24 mg/kg. Subsequent experiments showed that removing the ratio component reduced induction and clarified that high-dose responding was partly due to cross-component control. Chronic dosing produced tolerance to chlorpromazine, and abrupt withdrawal led to temporary behavioral disruptions resembling a withdrawal syndrome.

title: A scanning principle for auto-instructional devices1
SALIVARY CONDITIONING IN DOGS DURING FIXED-INTERVALREINFORCEMENT CONTINGENT UPON LEVER PRESSING
process: Interaction between operant and respondent conditioning—specifically
temporal (fixed-interval) respondent conditioning embedded within an operant contingency.
abstract: Four dogs were trained to press a lever for food under an FI 2-minute schedule while salivary responses were continuously recorded via implanted parotid duct tubing. Respondent salivation increased prior to food delivery, showing a temporal pattern similar to the operant lever-pressing curve (low immediately post-reinforcement, rising as reinforcement time approached). Salivary conditioning extinguished when reinforcement ceased and covaried positively with operant rate. A negative correlation between conditioned (CR) and unconditioned (UR) salivation suggested reciprocal modulation between anticipatory and consummatory responding.

title: Commercial liquid diet for animals in behavioral studies
STIMULUS FACTORS IN A VERSIVE CONTROLS:THE GENERALIZATION OF CONDITIONED SUPPRESSION
process: Conditioned suppression (CER) and stimulus generalization under aversive control; modulation by motivational operations.
abstract:
White Carneaux pigeons key-pecked for food on VI 2-min while 48-s tones (300–3400 Hz, 80 dB SPL) periodically occurred; the last 8 s of a 1000-Hz tone co-terminated with response-independent shock during training. After stable, complete suppression to the CS, shock was removed and generalization tests (varied tone frequencies) were run. Initial suppression generalized broadly and then sharpened systematically across sessions as suppression extinguished for nontraining tones, with a slight bias toward lower frequencies. A second experiment showed deprivation effects: at 70% body weight (higher motivation), gradients were very sharp (little generalization); after raising to 80%, gradients broadened. Thus, conditioned suppression generalizes and then narrows in extinction, and the breadth of generalization is inversely related to motivation for the ongoing appetitive behavior."Five pigeons were trained on temporally defined reinforcement schedules in which the duration of the reinforcement-available period (

title: THE INTERACTING EFFECTS OF DEPRIVATIONAND REIANFORCEMENT SCHEDULE
process: Conditioned suppression (aversive Pavlovian control over operant responding) and its stimulus generalization/gradient sharpening during extinction; modulation by motivation (deprivation) of ongoing operant strength.

abstract: Pigeons on VI food schedules received 48-s tones ending with 8-s shock. After complete suppression to the training tone, nonshocked generalization tests showed initially broad suppression that narrowed across extinction, with slightly greater generalization to lower frequencies. A second study varied deprivation: stronger motivation (lower body weight) yielded sharper, less-generalized suppression gradients.

title: Simple devices for liquid reward delivery
RATE-CHANGE EFFECTS DURING A PRE-SCHEDULE-CHANGE STIMULUS
process: Behavioral contrast and anticipatory rate modulation under multiple variable-interval schedules with discriminative (pre-schedule-change) stimuli.
abstract: Four pigeons were trained on a multiple VI 1 min / VI 10 min schedule where a 3-minute warning light preceded each schedule change. Response rate consistently decreased during the warning that preceded transition to the richer (VI 1) component and increased during the warning that preceded transition to the leaner (VI 10) component. These rate-change effects were interpreted in terms of reinforcement properties of schedule transitions, schedule contrast, or emotional/motivational processes.

title: BEHA VIORAL CONTRAST WITH FIXED-INTER VAL ANDLOW-RATE REINFORCEMENT'
abstract: Two experiments demonstrated behavioral contrast under fixed-interval (FI) and differential-reinforcement-of-low-rate (DRL) schedules. Pigeons showed higher response rates on FI and DRL components when alternated with extinction than when alternated with reinforcement. On FI, contrast effects were strongest early in the interval; on DRL, short interresponse times (IRTs) increased most. The findings indicate that behavioral contrast does not depend solely on differential reinforcement or punishment of specific IRTs.

title: A VOIDANCE CONDITIONING IN THE CHIMPANZEE
abstract: Clark (1961) demonstrated that chimpanzees can acquire and maintain avoidance behavior under the Sidman (free-operant) avoidance procedure. Six young male chimpanzees learned to postpone periodic shocks by pressing a lever, showing characteristic acquisition patterns similar to those observed in other species—initial bursts of responding followed by stabilized, well-spaced avoidance responses. Extended training produced reliable avoidance without general behavioral deterioration, suggesting that avoidance conditioning in chimpanzees follows principles consistent with operant processes across species.

title: THE OPERANT CONDITIONING OF CONVERSATION
process: Social operant conditioning of sequential behavior
abstract: Four experiments tested whether the order of speakers in small-group conversation can be operantly conditioned. Triads (and one tetrad) discussed tasks requiring unanimous choices; “correct” feedback (reinforcement) was delivered contingent on specific conversational sequences (e.g., last two speakers in clockwise order, or ABC among three). Reinforcement increased target sequences above chance; in later studies with improved procedures (tones for feedback, one-way screen, colored-light guessing task), a single two-person subsequence (e.g., B→C) typically stabilized and dominated, suggesting shaping of a specific social response rather than a general positional rule. Observer reliability improved with higher reinforcement density. Results support that conversational turn order is a modifiable operant under group reinforcement.

title: OBSERVING RESPONSES IN PIGEONS
authors: Kelleher, Roger, T.; Riddle, W.C.; Cook, L.
process: stimulus-producing (observing) responses maintained by conditioned reinforcement under variable-ratio (VR) and extinction (EXT) conditions.
abstract: Pigeons were trained on an observing-response procedure in which periods of VR 100 and EXT alternated unpredictably during a white light (mixed stimulus). During VR 100, responses on a food-producing key were intermittently reinforced. Responses on an observing key produced a green light (positive stimulus) when VR 100 was in effect and a red light (negative stimulus) during EXT. The birds did not respond on either key during the negative stimulus but did respond on the food-producing key when the positive stimulus appeared. Observing responses were maintained under FR schedules up to a maximum ratio value, after which only food-producing responses occurred. When observing responses no longer produced stimuli, rates fell to zero. Prolonged exposure to FR 20 led to higher observing rates during EXT than VR 100. Chlorpromazine decreased overall responding but markedly increased observing-response rates, except during observing-response extinction sessions.

title: Concurrent generalization gradients for food-controlled and shock-controlied behavior
abstract: In the presence of a bright light, monkeys were trained to press a lever to avoid shock and to pull a chain for food reward. After gradients of generalization to other light intensities had been determined for each response, gradients were subsequently secured after training in a brightness discrimination and under several free-shock conditions. The following results were obtained: (1) Generalization gradients prior to discrimination training were much steeper for the food-controlled response than for the shock-controlled response. This finding was confirmed in another study in which rats served as subjects. (2) After discrimination training, both gradients became much steeper, but the avoidance gradient still showed more generalized responding than that of reward. (3) After a period of continuous testing with all the different test intensities, the two gradients became even steeper. In addition, differences between the two gradients virtually disappeared. (4) The intermittent delivery of free shocks during a previously non-shocked light intensity radically affected the shape of the avoidance gradient, just as the addition of an avoidance contingency did during the same, previously non-shocked, light intensity.

title: Sound-resistant housing for experimental chambers
THE CONDITIONING OF TEXTUAL RESPONSESUSING "EXTRINSIC" REINFORCERS
authors: Staats, A.W.; Staats, C.K.; Schutz, R.E.; Wolf, M.
abstract: Six 4-year-olds completed a programmed-text reading task that built from single words to sentences and short “stories.” In No-Reinforcement phases (social praise only), children quickly disengaged and text acquisition stalled. Introducing extrinsic reinforcement (edibles, small trinkets, and tokens exchangeable for prizes) restored engagement and produced steady gains in the number of new texts acquired per 45-min session, yielding learning curves analogous to operant conditioning records. Results suggest textual behavior in early reading can be effectively established and maintained with tangible/token reinforcement, with procedures (picture prompts, discrimination “loops”) that minimize guessing and bring responding under textual stimulus control.

title: VARIABLE-INTERVAL ESCAPE FROM STIMULIACCOMPANIED BY SHOCKS
process: Negative reinforcement via escape/avoidance maintained by conditioned aversive stimuli
abstract: Three rats pressed a bar to terminate irregularly spaced shock series; a successful press produced a fixed “time-out” with no shocks. In experimental sessions, a tone or light accompanied the shock series; in control sessions, no exteroceptive signal was present though shock contingencies were identical. Stable escape responding was maintained by conditioned aversive stimulation: response rates were higher with signals than without, decreased as the mean inter-shock interval increased, and fell when time-outs were shorter than ~60 s. A reliable session “warm-up” (initial delay then acceleration) indicated that some shock exposure was required to establish the supporting state. Discrimination between shock vs. no-shock periods (relative responding) depended on the ratio of inter-shock interval to time-out duration.

title: Rack for cumulative-response recorders
EXTEROCEPTIVE CONTROL OF FIXED-INTERVALRESPONDING
process: Stimulus control and temporal discrimination under fixed-interval schedules
abstract: Two pigeons were studied under fixed-interval (FI) schedules of food reinforcement to examine how exteroceptive “clock” stimuli affect temporal control of responding. The visual stimuli (colored lights changing in fixed order) provided discrete temporal cues across the interval. When light changes were response-independent, the stimuli came to exert nearly complete control over responding—pigeons pecked almost exclusively during the final light period. When light changes were response-dependent, responding reflected both the discriminative and reinforcing effects of light changes, showing intermediate control. Results suggest strong stimulus control of temporal responding by exteroceptive cues, with evidence of additional temporal discrimination at longer intervals.

title: Technique for reinforcing either of two organisms with a single food magazine
The alteration of behavior in a special classroom situation
abstract: Unproductive classroom behavior was eliminated in two emotionally disturbed boys by removing social consequences of the behavior. Behavior which was more adequate and efficient with respect to social and scholastic adjustment was shaped and maintained with social reinforcers.

title: SOME OBSERVATIONS ON THE ADVENTITIOUSREINFORCEMENT OF DRINKING UNDER FOODREINFORCEMENT
process: Adventitious (superstitious) reinforcement under variable-interval food schedules.
abstract: Clark (1962) investigated the adventitious reinforcement of drinking in rats responding under variable-interval (VI) food schedules. Strong post-reinforcement drinking emerged rapidly when short VI intervals and close proximity between lever and water tube were present. Attempts to disrupt the behavior using conjunctive inter-response-time contingencies or fixed-ratio schedules were largely ineffective; the behavior returned under VI conditions. However, increasing the lever–water distance or reducing short intervals prevented its emergence. The study demonstrated that superstitious drinking, once established, is highly resistant to change and is governed by the temporal proximity of reinforcement and collateral responses.

title: A tape recorder for instructional and other behavioral research1
GENERALIZATION AND DISCRIMINATION AS AFUNCTION OF THE SD-SA INTENSITY DIFFERENCE
process: Stimulus generalization and discrimination along an auditory intensity continuum
abstract: Pierrel and Sherman (1962) examined auditory-intensity discrimination and generalization in rats by varying the difference between SD and SA intensities (10 dB, 20 dB, and 30 dB). Smaller SD–SA differences required longer training to achieve stable discrimination. During generalization tests with multiple SA intensities, response gradients initially peaked away from the SD and SA but later stabilized with maxima at the SD intensity. Gradients declined more steeply on the SA side, indicating asymmetrical stimulus control. The study demonstrated that the precision and shape of generalization gradients are inversely related to SD–SA separation magnitude.

title: Elimination of undesired escape from foot shock
THE EFFECT OF DRUGS ON A FIXED-RATIOPERFORMANCE SUPPRESSED BY A PRE-TIME-OUTSTIMULUSi1
authors: Ferster, C.B.; Appel, J.B.; Hiss, R.A.
process: Fixed-ratio performance under aversive stimulus control
abstract: Ferster, Appel, and Hiss (1962) studied how several drugs affected pigeons’ fixed-ratio (FR) responding when a pre-time-out stimulus (a red light) suppressed performance. During the red light, responses produced time-outs; withholding responses allowed uninterrupted completion of the FR schedule. Larger FRs produced stronger suppression (“FR strain”). Administration of amobarbital, pentobarbital, chlorpromazine, and d-amphetamine markedly increased responding under these strained conditions, restoring more typical FR patterns. High doses reduced rates only briefly post-injection. The results suggest these drugs disrupt suppressive control by the pre-time-out stimulus rather than create new behavior, effectively normalizing disrupted FR performance.

title: DISTRIBUTIONAL PROPERTIES OF OPERANT-LEVELLOCOMOTION IN THE RAT
process: Operant-level locomotion; effects of access limitation (motivating operation) on response patterning—primarily reducing interburst intervals (IBIs).
abstract: Four rats had continuous access to activity wheels first, then access for 1 hr per day, and, subsequently, continuous access. Limiting S's access to the wheel substantially increased the total frequency of running. A distributional analysis of response duration, burst duration, and interburst interval showed that the increased frequency arose almost entirely from a shortening of the interval between successive bursts. In contrast, speed of the individual response and number of responses per burst changed only negligibly. If S were running, the probability that it would either stop or continue did not differ appreciably for the conditions of continuous or limited access to the wheel. But if S were not running, the probability that it would start running was appreciably greater for limited than for continuous access.

title: A simple method for reliably coating intracranial electrodes
CLASSICAL AVOIDANCE WITHOUT A WARNINGSTIMULUS
abstract: White rats were scheduled to be shocked every 15 sec; but they were given a limited time interval between shocks when they could prevent the next scheduled shock from occurring if they pressed a lever. The duration of this limited avoidance period was varied, as was its location within the interval between scheduled shocks. Response rate, shock frequency, and the temporal distribution of lever presses were examined. Conditions were generated in which the formation of a temporal discrimination prevented the animals from maintaining successful avoidance behavior.

title: EFFECTS OF dl-AMPHETAMINE UNDER CONCURRENTVI DRL REINFORCEMENT
process: Operant performance under concurrent reinforcement schedules (VI–DRL)
abstract: Three adult, food-deprived rats were given IP injections of dl-amphetamine sulfate under DRL and concurrent VI DRL reinforcement schedules. The drug results were as follows: (1) The IRT distributions of DRL responses shifted to the left, but some temporal discrimination remained. (2) The IRT distributions of VI responses shifted slightly to the left. (3) The distinguishing characteristics of VI and DRL IRT distributions were preserved. (4) The frequency distribution of number of VI responses between two consecutive DRL responses was relatively unaffected. (5) Over-all response rates on the two components of the concurrent schedules increased more or less proportionately. These findings imply that the primary behavioral effect of dl-amphetamine was a motor excitatory one. The drug’s disruption of timing behavior was not due to a derangement of internal timing mechanisms, nor to interference with the topography or pattern of behavior. Rather, it might be a secondary result of the accelerated emission of overt behavior patterns mediating the temporal spacing of DRL bar presses.

title: An Experimental Outline for Building and Exploring Multi-Operant Behavior Repertoires
STIMULUS FUNCTIONS IN CHAINED FIXED-INTERVALSCHEDULES
abstract: This study examined how different stimulus arrangements affect responding under a three-component chained fixed-interval (FI) schedule with pigeons. When a single stimulus was correlated with all components (a tandem schedule), response rates accelerated positively across intervals. When distinct stimuli were correlated with each component in a fixed order, birds paused for long durations in the first component, responded slowly in the second, and accelerated responding in the latter components. However, when the sequence of stimuli varied across trials, acceleration occurred in all components. Because the reinforcement contingencies were constant across procedures, the performance differences were attributed solely to the discriminative and conditioned reinforcing functions of the stimuli and their sequencing.

title: INDEPENDENCE OF CONCURRENT RESPONDINGMAINTAINED BY INTERVAL SCHEDULES OFREINFORCEMENT
process: Concurrent schedules of reinforcement and response independence.
abstract: Catania investigated how pigeons respond when two independent interval schedules operate concurrently on separate keys, comparing performance with and without a changeover delay (COD). Under conc VI 3 (mult VI 3 EXT) and conc VI 3 FI 6 arrangements, the COD prevented immediate reinforcement following a switch between keys. With the COD, each key maintained response patterns similar to when its schedule was programmed alone: steady responding under VI, high responding during the VI component of the multiple schedule, and scalloping under FI. Without the COD, behavior on one key often came under the control of reinforcers programmed for the other key, producing interaction and loss of characteristic interval performance. The study demonstrated that the COD promotes independence between concurrent responses and clarified relations among local response patterns, overall rate, and reinforcement frequency.

title: BEHAVIOR IN A NOVEL SITUATION AS INFLUENCED BYTHE IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING ENVIRONMENT'
process: Behavioral organization in novelty / effects of environmental history (stimulus complexity) on exploratory and self-maintenance responses.
abstract: Woods examined how rats’ behavior in a novel closed field (30″ square) depends on the immediately preceding 24-hr environment: free/complex, restricted, or standard lab cage. Using 5-sec time sampling over 24 minutes with exhaustive categories (sniffing, locomotion, grooming, freezing, lying/sitting, miscellaneous), he found large group differences. Sniffing generally declined over time, with a faster drop for animals coming from the free/complex environment; grooming increased over time, was more frequent in free-reared rats, and often showed cyclic waxing–waning. Notably, only free-reared animals sometimes lay down/slept in the final 9 minutes. Restricted and lab-cage rats showed briefer, more frequent behavioral shifts (shorter runs), whereas free-reared rats produced longer bouts of non-sniffing behavior later in the session. The study highlights immediate environmental history (especially stimulus complexity) as a determinant of behavioral organization in novelty and advocates time-sampling for profiling whole-organism behavior.

title: A FACILITATIVE EFFECT OF PUNISHMENTON UNPUNISHED BEHAVIOR
abstract: Two pigeons pecked under a multiple schedule with alternating 3-min red and green components; both components arranged VI 3-min food. During several phases, every peck in red produced electric shock (≈20 ms AC; intensities 1.35, 2.5, 3.6 mA). Punishment in red reliably decreased punished responding and produced behavioral contrast: the unpunished VI rate in green increased, with larger increases at higher shock intensities. When punishment was removed, red responding showed a transient overshoot and green rates declined, then recovered depending on conditions. Replacing red VI with extinction while removing punishment yielded a decrease then increase in green responding, separating effects of shock from reinforcement frequency. Local patterns showed high green rates early in the component with later within-component suppression.

title: SOME EFFECTS OF RESPONSE COST UPONHUMAN OPERANT BEHAVIOR
process: Effects of response cost/punishment on schedule-controlled performance; induction of FI temporal patterning and behavioral contrast-like adjustments via negative contingencies.
abstract: Across three experiments with human observers detecting brief visual signals, Weiner added a per-response point loss (“cost”) to VI and FI schedules that delivered 100 points per correct detection. Under VI (1, 3, 9 min), cost reliably reduced response rates while largely preserving the VI-typical constancy; effects held regardless of whether cost or no-cost came first. Under FI 1-min, FI scalloping emerged only with cost; without cost, responding was approximately constant within intervals (VI-like). Cost effects were reversible: removing cost restored prior no-cost baselines. By alternately scheduling cost/no-cost within FI intervals (e.g., 30-s or 15-s segments), the study produced classic FI irregularities (bites, knees, double scallops, run-throughs). Overall, response cost is a potent determinant of human schedule performance.

title: A restraining device for psychophysiological experimentation with dogs1
INTERLOCKING SCHED ULES OF REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Four male pigmented rats were exposed to a procedure designed to investigate the relation between several performance measures and a schedule continuum ranging from FR 36 to FI 2 through four intermediate interlocking schedules. On all schedules, each subject developed a stable, generally break-and-run performance. Analysis of cumulative records, post-reinforcement pauses, and running rates showed a continuum of performance related to the schedule continuum.

title: Operandum
DELAYED ALTERNATION IN THE PIGEON
abstract: Pigeons were studied in a delayed-response task requiring alternation of key pecks on two response keys, with blackout delays of 1–10 seconds between choices. Accuracy remained well above chance at all delays, though it was generally lowest at 1 and 10 seconds. Postural orientation during delays appeared to mediate accurate responding. The shape of the delay–accuracy function was discussed in terms of potential confounds involving stimulus traces and aversive time-out effects.

title: INTERACTIONS BETWEEN THE DISCRIMINA TIVEAND AVERSIVE PROPERTIES OF PUNISHMENT
process: Discriminative control and aversive control of punishment on FI schedules
abstract: On FI schedules, the authors arranged response-contingent electric shock in specific quarters of each interval to disentangle punishment’s discriminative vs. aversive functions. Mild shocks, when paired with extinction portions, acted as S^Δ and suppressed responding; when paired with reinforcement portions, they acted as S^D and elevated responding. As shock intensity increased, aversiveness amplified suppression in extinction-paired periods and attenuated (but did not abolish) enhancement in reinforcement-paired periods. Termination of S^Δ punishment produced compensatory post-S^Δ response bursts, unlike a neutral S^Δ (green light). Thus, punishment’s effect depends on both its discriminative history and aversive magnitude.

title: Another simple interval-programming circuit1
Response patterns following manipulandum change
FOOD SATIATION IN THE PIGEON
process: Motivational control of operant responding by food deprivation and satiation (satiation functions and deprivation effects).
static-equation-definitions: N = cumulative amount (number of food units / reinforcers) ingested during the satiation session at elapsed time t; K = proportionality (intake-rate) constant; t = elapsed eating time since onset of the satiation session; n = shape exponent (n = 1 yields the linear special case N = Kt, i.e., a straight-line cumulative-intake curve at constant rate K, which is the form the paper's data predominantly support; n < 1 would give the negatively accelerated curvilinear form Skinner reported for rats but Reese & Hogenson did NOT find in pigeons). Reconstructed from the corrupted fragment "N=Ktn,"; NOT read from the scanned original. Competing candidate: the printed relation may have been the simple linear N = Kt, with the trailing "n" an OCR/subscript artifact rather than a free exponent, since the authors classified curve shapes descriptively (~64% straight with abrupt stop) rather than fitting a power law. Variable identity (amount eaten vs. responses) is reconstructed, not confirmed.
abstract: Eight pigeons were permitted to eat to satiation after systematically increasing deprivation intervals (5–191 hr), and two others were tested at prescribed percentages of free-feeding weight. Across 110 sessions, most satiation curves were linear with abrupt stops (≈64%), fewer were linear with gradual stops, and none were fully curvilinear as in Skinner’s rat data. Pecking rates were constant until eating ceased abruptly at about 85% of free-feeding weight. Weight data showed predictable losses with deprivation and partial recovery after each satiation, with a consistent separation between pre- and post-feeding weights.

title: REDUCTION OF SHOCK FREQUENCY ASREINFORCEMENT FOR A VOIDANCE BEHA VIOR
process: Free-operant avoidance maintained by negative reinforcement via shock-frequency reduction
abstract: Rats had access to two levers, each controlling its own free-operant avoidance schedule (independent shock–shock and response–shock timers). Many animals initially pressed one lever predominantly, which already cut overall shock density roughly in half; alternation across levers further reduced shock frequency. Conditioning occurred rapidly when the shock–shock interval was short (e.g., 5 s), and changing the response–shock interval on one lever shifted responding to the other, with effects reversing when schedules were restored. Inter-response-time functions showed temporal discrimination (low short-pause responding, rising with time). Findings support “reduction of shock frequency” as the primary reinforcer in avoidance.

title: EFFECTS OF CHLORPROMAZINE ON APPETITIVE ANDAVERSIVE COMPONENTS OF A MULTIPLE SCHEDULE'
process: Multiple schedule performance under concurrent appetitive
abstract: A multiple schedule with both appetitive (food) and avoidance (shock) components was maintained in two dogs to study the effects of chlorpromazine (CPZ). Both soluble and sustained-release (“Spansule”) forms of CPZ produced comparable dose–response functions despite differing dosing procedures. Low doses slightly increased response rates on food-reinforced components while leaving avoidance responding largely unchanged. Higher doses depressed responding on both components approximately equally. The study discusses interpretive issues in comparing drug effects across schedules and between appetitive and aversive contingencies.

title: THE QUAIL, Coturnix coturnix, AS A LABORATORY ANIMAL
process: Acquisition and maintenance of operant behavior (pecking) under food reinforcement
abstract: The quail Coturnix coturnix is described as an ideal laboratory bird: small, hardy, docile, inexpensive, and easy to maintain. Reese and Reese demonstrated that the pecking operant can be conditioned rapidly with minimal deprivation and that quail learn visual and temporal discriminations with remarkable speed. They adapted well to laboratory conditions, showed stable responding despite distractions, and could perform under continuous, fixed-ratio, and fixed-interval schedules. Their rapid maturation and tolerance for short deprivation periods make them suitable for operant conditioning research, comparative studies, and teaching demonstrations.

title: AN ADJUSTING AVOIDANCE SCHEDULE'
process: Avoidance conditioning under variable response–shock contingencies
recursive-equation-definitions: Unverifiable fragment. The source (Sidman, 1962, JEAB 5(2):271-277) is available only as scanned page images; only the abstract is machine-readable. This is a procedural free-operant avoidance report, not a quantitative-modeling paper, and is unrelated to the matching-law / GML / signal-detection canon. The fragment matches no canonical EAB model and contains an undefined symbol z. It is also mislabeled "recursive": it is a closed-form expression linear in n with no T_{n-1} dependence, hence not a true recurrence. If taken at face value, n would index successive lever presses and the "5" would reflect the 5 s of accrued "safe time" per press confirmed in the abstract, but no such displayed equation could be verified in the source. Retained as a traceability echo only, at very low confidence; do not treat as a validated model.
abstract: Sidman developed an “adjusting avoidance” schedule in which each lever press postponed shock by 5 s, allowing rats to accumulate up to 50 s of safety. This design eliminated differential reinforcement for long pauses, resulting in response probabilities largely independent of elapsed time since the last press. When a warning stimulus signaled proximity to shock (≤ 5 s), rats increased responding near the warning period and spent more time closer to shock, demonstrating control by temporal cues. The procedure produced rapid conditioning and revealed that shock-frequency reduction, rather than temporal discrimination alone, governs avoidance behavior.

title: PROGRAMMING STIMULI IN MATCHING TO SAMPLE
process: discrimination learning and transfer of stimulus control
abstract: Preschool and first-grade children learned matching-to-sample using a teaching-machine program that introduced a sequence of gradually harder discriminations. Training with these successive approximations was far more efficient than training on the final (criterion) discrimination alone. Error rates depended jointly on the “step size” between consecutive discriminations and on how long children trained at each step. The work highlights how programming stimulus control (and when to advance steps) governs errors and efficiency, with implications for both theory (continuity/discontinuity, stimulus control) and instructional design.

title: RESPONSE LATENCY AS A FUNCTION OFREINFORCEMENT SCHEDULE1
abstract: "Four rats were trained to press and hold a key during a light and release it upon onset of a tone, with water reinforcement following correct releases. Reinforcement schedules were systematically varied (CRF, intermittent, extinction). Median response latency and its variability were inversely related to reinforcement frequency: lower reinforcement probabilities produced longer and more variable reaction times. Extinction produced the greatest latency increases, suggesting a graded relationship between reinforcement density and response speed stability."]

title: RESPONSE LATENCY AS A FUNCTION OF AMOUNTOF REINFORCEMENT
abstract: Four food-deprived rats were trained to press and hold a telegraph key in the presence of a light and to release it upon hearing a tone, which produced a sucrose solution as reinforcement. After establishing a stable baseline with 20% sucrose, concentrations were reduced to 5% and 0%. Decreases in sucrose concentration produced systematic increases in both the median and variability of response latency, with the greatest change at 0%. These results indicate that response latency is inversely related to the amount of reinforcement, paralleling effects previously observed for reinforcement frequency.

title: EFFECTS OF OPERANT REINFORCEMENT ON THE GSR1
authors: Mandler, G.; Preven, D.W.; Kuhlman, C.K.
process: Attempted operant conditioning of an autonomic respondent (GSR); observed effect aligns more with stimulus-controlled arousal/activation than response-contingent reinforcement.
abstract: Nine undergraduates completed 11 daily sessions measuring GSR (≥500-ohm drops in ≤2 s). Sessions 2–9 included a 10-min no-reinforcement control followed by 20-min periods in which each qualifying GSR turned on a red light (putative operant reinforcer). Sessions 10–11 were extinction. Across subjects, there was no orderly acquisition indicating operant conditioning of the GSR. However, GSR rates were reliably higher during reinforcement than control for participants with low baseline (operant) GSR rates (“stabiles”), but not for those with high baselines (“labiles”). Conductance (arousal) rose during control, spiked at reinforcement onset, then remained elevated, and rose further during extinction, suggesting the reinforcement period functioned as a contextual activator rather than a contingent reinforcer of GSR.

title: A response key for use with projection-type display units1
A TRACKING PROCEDURE FOR DETERMININGTHE CAT'S FREQUENCY DISCRIMINATION
authors: Elliot, D.N.; Frazier, L.; Riach, W.
process: Operant discrimination learning under a feedback (tracking
abstract: Cats were trained to discriminate between a steady 1000 Hz tone and a 3 Hz frequency-modulated (“warbling”) tone using a feedback (tracking) operant conditioning procedure. Pressing one of two bars during the steady tone produced food on a variable-ratio (VR) schedule; pressing the other during the warble changed the tone back to steady. Early training showed poor auditory stimulus control because of rapid, indiscriminate responding. Introducing inter-press time-outs (TOs) and light cues signaling the correct bar and TO periods markedly improved discrimination. Although the method required many sessions, it minimized the “experimental neurosis” seen in avoidance conditioning and may be superior for long-term auditory threshold studies.

title: A relay sequencing device for scrambling grid shock1
FI LENGTH AND PERFORMANCE ON AN FIFR CHAIN SCHEDULE OF REINFORCEMENT
authors: Hanson, H.M.; Cambell, E.H.; Witoslawski, J.J.
process: Fixed-interval (FI) temporal control within a chained schedule of reinforcement.
abstract: In a chained FI–FR schedule, manipulating the length of the FI component produced changes confined almost entirely to the FI performance; increasing the interval length increased the total number of responses emitted per reinforcement. The configuration of the fixed-interval scallop was clearly modified as the interval length was increased, with the larger intervals becoming flatter (i.e., a larger proportion of the total responses earlier in an interval). Measurement of the postreinforcement pause is suggested as a possible indicator of fixed-interval scalloping.

title: PRODUCING EITHER POSITIVE OR NEGATIVETENDENCIES TO A STIMULUS ASSOCIATED WITH SHOCK
abstract: A technique is described in which rats are pretrained with reinforcement to bar press. Each bar press was associated with a tone. This tone was later paired with one of two aspects of an electric shock—either at the onset or at the end of the shock—in a situation in which the shock was inescapable. These animals were retested in the operant situation under extinction, but with the tone present as a conditioned reinforcer. Animals for which the tone was associated with shock onset extinguished quickly, whereas those for which the tone was paired with shock termination extinguished more slowly.

title: A combined manipulandum-reinforcement arrangement1
Continuous recordings of revolving-cage activity units
CONTROL OF THE BEHAVIOR OF SCHIZOPHRENICPATIENTS BY FOOD'
process: Operant conditioning with food reinforcement: extinction of socially maintained problem behavior
and establishment of cooperative responding via programmed contingencies.
abstract: Ayllon & Haughton (1962) used operant procedures to control behavior of 45 chronic psychiatric inpatients on a closed ward by making food access contingent on specific responses. First, they withdrew all social attention for “refusal to eat,” which rapidly eliminated eating problems. They then added response requirements: a motor act (deposit a coin to enter the dining room) and later a social/cooperative act (two patients simultaneously press buttons to earn coins). With a 5-min access window, patients reliably acquired and maintained the chains without spoon/tube feeding or coercion; weights and health were largely stable. The study demonstrates that inadvertent social reinforcement can maintain “refusal to eat,” and that food functions as a powerful reinforcer to shape motor and social behavior in this population.

title: QUANTITA TIVE RELA TIONS BETWEEN A VOIDANCEBEHAVIOR AND PITUITARY-ADRENALCORTICAL ACTIVITY1
authors: Sidman, M.; Mason, J.W.; Brady, J.V.; Thach, J.
process: with parametric control via response–shock intervals and free-shock probes.
abstract: Sidman, Mason, Brady & Thach (1962) studied rhesus monkeys avoiding shock via lever pressing while measuring plasma 17-hydroxycorticosteroids (indexing pituitary–adrenal activity). Manipulating avoidance parameters showed steroid elevations covaried with both behavior and shock exposure. Shorter response–shock intervals increased avoidance rates and typically raised steroids; adding warning stimuli (discriminated avoidance) lowered response rates and steroid rises. Superimposing unavoidable “free” shocks increased both response rate and steroids; removing them reduced both. In extinction with constant free shocks (every 2 min), steroids declined as responding ceased, but surged when shock rate was briefly increased (every 20 s). Reinstating high-rate discriminated avoidance without shocks again elevated steroids. Thus, adrenal activation depends jointly on avoidance response rate and shock frequency.

title: MACHINE DEFINITION OF ONGOING SILENT ANDORAL READING RATE'
process: Observing/monitoring responses (a form of operant-controlled attending to textual stimuli).
abstract: Goldiamond (1962) introduced an apparatus that operationalizes ongoing silent and oral reading as a sequence of “monitoring responses.” A projected page is masked by an opaque loop with a moving transparent slit; each press of a microswitch advances the slit to reveal successive text segments (≈half-line frames). The device thereby defines reading rate as presses per time and brings it under experimental control. With this method, reading/monitoring rates proved highly stable and were sensitive to manipulations including item difficulty, signal-to-noise (defocus), schedule-based payoffs (e.g., DRL contingencies), age, and practice. The same framework generalizes to other visual monitoring tasks (e.g., complex displays), enabling training of selective attention to different regions of a stimulus.

title: The effect of multiple SΔ periods on responding on a fixed-interval schedule1
abstract: The effect of repeated interruption of FI responding by short SΔ presentations on the pattern of increasing frequency of responding through the interval has been studied. Although the SΔ profoundly changed the pattern of responding during their presentation, the general scalloped pattern of FI responding survived. The implication of these findings for understanding the role of chaining of responses in FI patterns is discussed. It is suggested that chaining is not a necessary condition for the scalloped pattern.

title: Instructions and stimulus categorizing in a measure of stimulus generalization1
abstract: In Experiment I, three groups of 20 Ss each were exposed to a light of 550 mμ (yellowish-green) for 60 sec and then viewed a random sequence of wavelengths with instructions to respond only to the original color. The instructions given the three groups were worded differently in an attempt to vary the strength of a set-to-discriminate assumed to be created by this procedure. The three groups produced similar gradients, each with a peak of responding at 540 mμ, in agreement with Kalish's (1958) published gradient for the 550 mμ standard stimulus value. It was suggested that the nature of the task is such that a strong discriminatory set is produced regardless of the wording of the instructions.A temporal analysis of the gradient as it develops during the testing revealed that initially the peak of responding occurs at 550 mμ; but as testing progresses, it shifts gradually in the direction of the shorter wavelengths (purer greens). Experiment II was performed to test the generality of the phenomenon of regression to the primary color. Two groups of 20 Ss each were tested for generalization following exposure to 510 mμ (bluish-green) and 525 mμ (pure green), respectively. We predicted that the 510 mμ gradient would reveal a progressive shift toward the longer wavelengths (purer greens), whereas the 525 mμ gradient would show no tendency to shift. The results were strikingly in accord with these predictions.We concluded that although a physiological process could not be ruled out, the verbal labeling of the standard stimulus value may well be responsible for the regression of the gradient toward the primary color.

title: The operant control of vocalization in the dog1
abstract: Control over the vocal responses of three dogs was established using operant-conditioning procedures. Several points of interest were observed in the data. First, fixed-ratio schedules of reinforcement generated a vocal response topography which was similar in detail to that of a “motor” bar-nosing response. Second, vocal responding was brought under the control of external visual stimuli as a result of differential reinforcement. Third, good stimulus control was maintained on a multiple schedule containing a vocal-response component and a bar-response component. Fourth, the stimulus control on the multiple schedule transferred with minimal disruption to a chain schedule requiring a sequence of 10 bar responses followed by 10 vocal responses. Fifth, because vocal and bar responses are not mutually exclusive, concurrent responding tended to develop on the chain schedule.These results were discussed with reference to the advisability of applying the terms operant and respondent to unconditioned behavior, and, particularly, to unconditioned verbal behavior.

title: The functional properties of a time out from an avoidance schedule1
abstract: Investigations are reported of some of the discriminative (cue) and reinforcing properties of stimuli (TOav) correlated with the discontinuation of a free-operant avoidance schedule. After several unsuccessful initial attempts to demonstrate the positively reinforcing effect of TOav, a special technique was developed. The subjects were trained by means of a free-operant avoidance procedure to press a lever and postpone electric shock; by pressing a second lever, they could produce a cue correlated with the TOav period. The importance of a distinct cue correlated with TOav was demonstrated in experiments in which this signal was eliminated from the procedure. The reinforcing function of the TOav period was explored by showing its effectiveness under various schedules of reinforcement.Other observations were made concerning the course of extinction of both TOav-producing responses and avoidance behavior.In further experiments in which TOav was used as a reinforcer, the TOav behavior was also brought under separate stimulus control. The development of the various discriminations involved in the resulting performance were described.

title: Time out from avoidance as a reinforcer: a study of response interaction1
abstract: Monkeys could either postpone shock by pressing a lever or pull a chain to produce a period of time out from the avoidance procedure. The period of time out proved to be an effective positive reinforcer. Certain features of the animals' behavior were attributed to interactions between the two responses.

title: Generalization gradients of inhibition following auditory discrimination learning1
abstract: A more direct method than the usual ones for obtaining inhibitory gradients requires that the dimension of the nonreinforced stimulus selected for testing be orthogonal to the dimensions of the reinforced stimulus. In that case, the test points along the inhibitory gradient are equally distant from the reinforced stimulus. An attempt was made to realize this condition by obtaining inhibitory gradients along the frequency dimension of a pure tone after discrimination training in which the nonreinforced stimulus was a pure tone (or tones), and the reinforced stimulus was either white noise or the absence of a tone. The results showed that some degree of specific inhibitory control was exerted by the frequency of the tone, although the gradients were broad and shallow in slope.A further experiment was conducted to see whether the modification of an excitatory gradient resulting from training to discriminate neighboring tones could arise from a simple interaction of inhibitory and excitatory gradients. The results indicated that it could not, since discrimination training produced a concentration of responding in the vicinity of the reinforced stimulus which cannot be derived from any plausible gradient of inhibition.

title: A simple flip-flop circuit
Additional techniques for producing multiple-schedule control in children, 12
abstract: The subjects in these experiments were 132 children, varying in age from 4 to 7 years. These experiments were designed to assess the efficacy of various multiple scheduling procedures in producing reliable stimulus control. The schedules studied were multiple fixed-ratio–extinction (mult FR EXT); multiple differential-reinforcement-of-other-behavior–fixed-ratio (mult DRO FR); multiple differential-reinforcement-for-low-rate–fixed-ratio (mult DRL FR); and multiple fixed-interval—fixed-ratio (mult FI FR). In addition other techniques were investigated, such as presenting FR's in blocks; increasing the size of the FR's; attaching a DRL to the FI members; temporarily shifting to new schedules; and adding an external clock to the FI's. These experiments yielded the following results.1.) Strong stimulus control was produced by mult FR EXT, mult DRO FR, and mult DRL FR schedules. Control for mult FR EXT was mediated principally by the individual stimuli, though on occasion it was dependent in part on the change of stimuli. The mult DRO FR was found to be highly useful for those children who had very high initial rates or who were generally uncooperative and unmanageable.2.) Contrary to a previous finding, some subjects were brought under stimulus control by means of mult FI FR schedules without the aid of additional procedures. Most, however, were not. Additional techniques found to augment the development of mult FI FR control included: (1) presenting FR's in blocks; (2) increasing the size of the FR's; (3) attaching a DRL to the FI component for a time and later removing it; and (4) shifting to a mult DRL FR, developing control, and then returning to the original mult FI FR.3.) Addition of an external clock to the FI components of the mult FI FR had several effects. Strongest control, including well-developed acceleratory patterns during the FI's, was developed in those subjects who had first been shifted from a regular mult FI FR to a mult FR EXT, brought under control, and then returned to the mult FI FR with the clock added. The added clock also produced strong control if it was present when the subject was first begun on a mult FI FR schedule. In some cases, the addition of the clock produced control in subjects who had not been controlled previously by the regular mult FI FR, but these were always subjects who had high rates. The addition of the clock first lowered the rate, then produced control.

title: Photograph of first Conference on the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
A student laboratory for operant conditioning
Inexpensive plug-in circuits1
A displacement-sensing, constant-torque response lever
Effects of deprivation upon counting and timing in rats
abstract: Two procedures were used in an investigation of the effects of deprivation upon counting and timing. Under the first procedure, fixed minimum interval (FMI), the rat received liquid reinforcement every time it pressed bar B after having waited a minimum of 5 sec following a press on bar A. Under the second procedure, fixed consecutive number (FCN), reinforcement was delivered every time the rat pressed bar B following a run of at least four consecutive responses on bar A.Water deprivation was varied over a set of values ranging from 4 to 56 hr. Deprivation had almost no effect on the waiting time in the FMI procedure, or on the number of responses per run in the FCN procedure. With both procedures, increasing deprivation shortened the pause between reinforcement and the next response. In the FCN procedure, the speed with which the runs were executed increased with increasing deprivation, although the number of responses in these runs was relatively unaffected.

title: Electroencephalographic correlations of temporally spaced responding and avoidance behavior
abstract: This study was undertaken to determine whether any EEG changes occurred during a multiple schedule of reinforcement consisting of repeated periods of avoidance behavior, a time-out (TO) period, and a period of differential reinforcement of low rates (DRL). The two monkeys were permanently implanted with bipolar electrodes in various subcortical areas. The EEG was recorded from these electrodes for several weeks before any behavioral training was undertaken. Training was then begun in the multiple schedule, and EEG recordings were taken frequently throughout the training period. When a stable performance level was achieved, drugs (dl-amphetamine and sodium pentobarbital) were introduced which disrupted the DRL performance but had little or no effect on avoidance behavior. The EEG recordings continued throughout these drug studies.The data indicate that the marked behavioral differences noted in each component of the schedule were not reflected in the EEG. However, the EEG did correlate with the general level of alertness of the animals during the various components. The drugs which differentially affected the behavior in the components of the schedule did not differentially affect the EEG, but they did change the brain-wave activity equally in all components. Finally, EEG changes correlated with the complex motor response of lever pressing were not observed.ImagesFig. 1.

title: Complex response patterns during temporally spaced responding
abstract: A series of experiments is reported in which two monkeys emitted complex response patterns, not specified by the experimental program, during the DRL component of a multiple schedule. Administration of sodium pentobarbital and dl-amphetamine, drugs which disrupted the DRL performance, were also observed to suppress these collateral responses.
